I should not, therefore, be ambitious of a rich mausoleum after my death, for the repose of my body ; nor do I desire a stately sepulchre, a beautiful urn, or that my name or actions should be engraven in marble ; I know this, that if I shall be miserable and unhappy hereafter, they will be but for my greater shame and reproach. Out of this life I can carry nothing but my good works ; 1 will not add unto my evil ones that of vain glory ; I will take heed whereon I set my heart, since the accomplishment of what I wish may be a punishment of my desires; if those things of the earth which I most love and desire should continue long, be taken from me, it is-a chastisement of my earthly affection ; and if 1 be permitted to enjoy them, I am fearful that they may be the temporal reward of some good work, which may either diminish or deprive me of the eternal.

What is Death ? þÿ Is it not the interruption of all our former appetites ? Do the dead hunger or thirst any more ? W ill beauty move their love ? Will the tablet or the harp> the richest wines or the most luxurious viands entice them beyond the bounds of temperance ? Load the coffin with gold ; clothe the skeleton with scarlet and ermine ! Will these awaken his avarice, or will these elevate his pride Surely, if the soul perceives at all the objects which surround the ruins of her recent dwelling, she perceives them but to recognize their utter vanity, and to feel that these are not the things which can any longer contribute to her happiness.

The Goodness of God. þÿ Whatever we enjoy is purely a free gift from our Creator ; but that we enjoy no more, can never sure be deemed an injury, or a just reason to question his infinite benevolence. All our happiness is owing to his goodness ; but that it is no greater, is owing only to ourselves ; that is, to our not having any inherent right to any happiness, or even to any existence at all. þÿ Family Whist. þÿ This is no more to be imputed to God, than the wants of a beggar to tiie person who has relieved him ; that had something, was owing to his benefactor ? but that he had no more only to his own original poverty. All-suffiency of Christ. þÿ Our necessities may be as many as the sands upon the seashore, our desires as boundless as the ocean, they encircle, and our hopes and aspirations as high as the heaven that looks down upon them ; but in Christ is a sufficiency of supply þÿ infinite, unfathomable, unexplored ; þÿ no sin beyond his power of deliverance, no tear he cannot dry, no wound he cannot heal, no soul that he is not willing and able to bless with the salvation of the gospel.

Sacred Truths. þÿ The fairest productions of human wit, after a lew perusals, like gathered flowers, wither in our hands, and lose their fragrancy ; but scripture precepts, like unfading plants of paradise, become, as we are accustomed to them, still more and more beautiful, their bloom appears to be daily heightened ; fresh odoars to be emitted and new sweets extracted from them. He who hath once tasted their excellencies, will desire to taste them again ; and he who tastes them oftenest, will relish them best.
A devout þÿSpirit. Without this, your imagination may be charmed, your sensibility excited, and your mind enriched ; but your heart will continue at þÿ enmity with God," and

Cure for a Passionate Temper. A merchant in London had a dispute with a Quaker, respecting the settlement of an account. The merchant was determined to bring the question into Court, a proceeding the Quaker deprecated, using every argument in his power to convince the merchant of his error ; but the latter was inflexible. þÿ Desirous to make a last effort, the Quaker called at his house one morning ; and inquired of the servant if his master was at home. The merchant hearing the inquiry, and knowing the voice, called aloud from the top of the stairs, þÿ tell the rascal 1 am not at þÿhome. The Quaker, looked up to him calmly, said, þÿ Well friend ; God put the in better þÿmind. The merchant, struck with the meekness of the reply and having more deliberately investigated the matter, became convinced that the Quaker was right and he wrong. He requested to see him. and after acknow. ledging his error, he said þÿ þÿ have I one question to ask you þÿ how wen? you able with such patience, various occa- on sions, to bear with my abuse þÿ? þÿ Friend, replied the Quaker, þÿ will I tell thee : I was naturally as hot and violent as thou art, I knew that thus to indulge was imprudent. I observed that men in a passion always speak loud ; and 1 thought that if I could control my voice, I should suppress my passion. 1 therefore made it a rule never to suffer my voice to rise above a certain key ; and by a careful observance of this rule, have with the blessing of God, entirely mastered
my natural þÿtemper.

Female Piety. The gem of all others which enriches the coronet of a þÿlady s character is unaffected piety. Nature may lavish much on tier person þÿ the enchantment of the countenance þÿ the grace of her mein, or the strength of her intellect, yet her loveliness is uncrowned, till piety throws around the whole, the sweetness and power, of her charms. She then becomes unearthly in desires and associations. þÿ The spell which bound her affections to the things below is broken, and she mounts on the silent wings of her fancy and hope to the habitation of God, where it is her delight to hold communication with the spirits that have been ransomed from the thraldom of earth and wreathed with a garland of glory. Her beauty may throw a magical charm over many ; þÿ Princes and conquerors may bow with admiration at the shrine of her love, to the said Mr. þÿWolff s the sons of science and poetry may embalm her memory in history and song yet her þÿ piety must be her ornament : her pearl. Her name must be written in tiie þÿ Book of þÿlife, while that when the mountains fade away, and every memento of earthly greatness is lost in the general wreck of nature, it may remain and swell the list of that mighty throng, which have been clothed with the mantle of righteousness, and their voice attuned to the melody of heaven. With such a treasure every lofty gratification on earth may be purchased : friendships will be doubly sweet, pain and sorrow shall Jose their sting, and the character will possess

a price far þÿ above þÿriches, life will be but a pleasant visit to earth, and death the entrance upon joyful a and perpetual home. And when the notes of the last trump shall be heard, and sleeping millions awake to judgment, its possessor shall be presented þÿ faultless before the throne of God with exceeding joy and a crown of glory that shall never wear away." 8uch is piety. Like a tender flower, planted in the fertile soil of þÿwoman heart, s it grows, expanding its foliage and imparting its fragrance to all around, till transplanted it is set to bloom in perpetual vigour and unlading beauty in the Paradise of God. Follow this star, it will light you through every labyrinth in the wilderness of life gild þÿ the gloom that will gather around you in a dying hour, and bring you safely over the tempestuous Jordan of death, into the heaven of promised and settled rest.

ECONOMY IN A FAMILY. There is nothing which goes so far towards placing people beyond the reach of poverty, as economy in the management of their domestic atluirs. It is as much impossible to get a ship across the Atlantic with half a dozen butts started, or as many bolt holes in her bottom, as to conduct the concerns of a family without economy It matters not whether a man furnish little or much foi iiis family, if there is a continual leakage in the kitchen, or in the parlor it runs away, he knows not how, and that demon, waste, cries more, like the horse leech's daughter, until lie that provides has no more to give. It is the husband's duty to bring into the house, and it is the duty of the with to see that nothing goes wrongfully out of it ; not the least article, however unimportant in itself, for it establishes a precedent ; nor, under any pretence, for it opens the door for ruin to stalk in, and he seldom leaves an opportunity unimproved. A man gets a wife to look after his affairs, and to assist him in his journey through life, to educate and prepare his children lor a proper station in life, and not to dissipate his property. The husband's interest should be the wife's care, and her greatest ambition cany her no further than his welfare and happiness, together with that of her children. 'I his should he her sole aim, and the thtre ot her exploits in the bosom of her family, where she may do as much towaids making a fortune as lie possibly can do in the counting-room or work-shop. It is not

the money earned that makes a man wealthy ; it is what is saved from Iiis earnings A good and prudent husband makes a deposite of the fruits of his labor with his best þÿfriend and if that friend be not true to him, what has lie to

hope; if lie dare not place confidence in the companion of his bosom, where is he to place it? A wife acts not for herself only, hut she is the agent of many she loves, and she is bound to act for their good, and not for her own gratification. Her husband's good is the end at which she should aim þÿ Ids approbation is her reward. Self gratification in dress, or indulgence in appetite, or more company than his purse can well entertain ; are equally pernicious. The first adds vanity to extravagance þÿ the second fastens a doctor's bill to a long butcher's account, and the latter brings intemperance, the worst of all evils, in its train. þÿ Anon.

Divorces in Georgia þÿ A poor unfortunate wight, whose local habitation is in the State ot Georgia, but whose name we know not, recently applied to one of the Courts lor a divorce. Truly honest in all his dealings, he was unwilling to deprive his wife of her share of his property, to which she was entitled under the laws, and therefore, when called upon for an inventory of his real and personal estate, he presented the following very satisfactory schedule : One-fifth part of an undivided tract of Land, containing two hundred and twenty-three acres. One Pine Chest, containing my wearing apparel. A very small lot of experience. A still less quantity of good judgment. A small share of Temperance, and A great deal less of Prudence. A small stock of industry, mixed with A small stock of Economy As much Honesty as was sufficient to keep a man poor. And Fortitude sufficient for any man in no better circumstances. The above is a complete schedule of all the property that 1 owned, held or claimed, on the day that I was unfortunately married, which was ou the 23d of September, 1813 What action has been taken by the Court we know not, and we are curious to learn what portion of Ins estate was given to his wife.

Acoustic Chair þÿ This invention is of the size of a large library chair, with a high back, to which are affixed two barrels for sound, and at the extremity of each is a perforated plate, that collects sound, i to a paraboloid vase, from every part of the room, and impresses it more sensibly on the ear, bv giving it only a small quantity of air. The converse end of the vase serves to reflect the voice, and to render it more distinct. By means of sufficient tubes, this chair might be made to convey intelligence from St. James' to the House of Lords and Commons, and even from London to the King at Windsor. Marvellous as this may seem, the idea is not a novelty; it is hut another confirmation of the saving of Solomon, that there is nothing new under the sun. M. hard, in his excellent work on the ear, tells us that Aristotle (who was physician to Alexander the Great) invented a trumpet for his master which was capable of convey ing orders to rather more than twelve miles, And I may remark, bearing in mind, too, that both A lei neon and Hippocrates are said to have invented car trumpets, the ancient do not seem to have been so ignoiant of acoustic as some in our day have represented þÿthem. . Another invention of mine is a trumpet with two apertures, one to he inserted info th® meatus, and the other into the þÿmouth. -Cut til on the Ear,

New Orleans. þÿ We learn from New Orleans, under date of the 18th April, that the Banks of that city have begun to issue ninety day post notes, and that the best sixty day paper would be received in exchange for them. The New Urleans True American has the following startling notice of the aggregate amount ofthe recent failures in that city: " The gross amount of failures in this city, from a careful estimate, is reckoned at 97 millions. This was up to the 4th inst. It is now considerably over 100 millions. In the end, the deficit will be over 60 millions, even if the property 111 existence be sold at the most favorable rates. Here then we have a credit copital whose value depends entirely upon time and the energy of our people. Does not this fact speak volumes against the system by which we have been building up our prosperity ! It is a deceitful ground on which we have been operating. W e now find it giving way beneath our feet, involving all who have rested their faith upon its solidity in one general ruin. Time will prove to us that a credit capital has been the cause of all our misfortunes, and that no country can make a permanent progress if she depends upon it. As the facts come from abroad, we shall revert to this point. The only remedy that remains for us now, is to abolish the system of credits, and turn to the never-failing sources of actual capital as the only true means of commercial prosperity. " The bills of the banking honse of Yeatman,

Woods & Co., we hear, were protested yesterday at the Bank of Louisiana. This will create great distress with the holders of their paper in this city ; though we hope that the amount in circulation is not large The greatest loss to be experienced will be felt in Tennessee, if the house has failed."

A Cause þÿ The Natchez Courier suppose that " upwards 10,000 slaves were sold in the State of Mississippi, from 1st November, 1835, to the same period in 1830, on a credit , that is to say, for the notes and acceptances of merchants and planters The value of these slaves could not have been less than ten millions of dollars. The planters, then, created a debt for slaves alone, to be paid out of the crop of 1830, equal to ten millions of dollars."

Ludicrous Mistaki:. þÿ Sir Francis Head, Governor of Upper Canada, was travelling a short time since in the Western part of the province on horseback, wiili his þÿsecretary. O11 approaching a small village Inn, they took accidentally different roads, and the Governor arriving first, his horse was found to answer very nearly the description of one placarded in the bar room as stolen His Excellency, being incognito, was apprehended and brought before Justice Writetnedown, when the following dialogue ensued:--" There is a complaint lodged against you for stealing the horse now in your possession." Governor. Very well, sir. Justice. Where are you from ? þÿ Governor. I am from Toronto, and on mv way to Detroit. J ustice. What's your name ? Governor. My name is Francis Bond Head. Justice. Well now that must be an all fired Ire, for that's our Governor's name and he don't steal horses. Governor. It is true, sir, and I happen to be at this time the Governor of Upper Canada, but I don't know that I look like a horse thief. At this stage of the proceedings, his Secretary came up, the prisoner was identified as the true representative of his Majesty, and instantly discharged from durance, by the astonished magistrate, who swore hard at his stars, tlrat he was so blind as to mistake a Canadian Governor for a horse thief.

MEXICO AND THE UNITED STATES. Mexico. þÿ We have received from Mexico, by way of Havana, the Diario of the 3d April, in which we find the following document, which, under present circumstances, is very interesting. At that date, there was no discussion of the Presidential election, and every thing seemed quiet in Mexico.

Jfclt 3aXJs3XTB3 A'TttS. Office of Foreign Affairs General Government il To His Excellency the Secretary of foreign Affairs of the United States. Palace of the National Government at Mexico, March 21, 1837. The undersigned, senior officer, charged with the foreign affairs of the Mexican Republic, lias the honor to address the Secretary of the same department of the United States of America, in order to express to him the just surprise with which the President ad interim of this Republic has seen the annunciation, in the New Orleans Bee of the 13th of the present month, of the acknowledgment by the Congress of the United States of the independence proclaimed by the insurgents the Texas, and the subsequent appointment by of Government of Mr. Alcee l.abrancbe to be Minister Plenipotentiary to the pretended republic. Measures thus premature have caused the more astonishment in the Mexican Government that it had no reason to believe that they would he adopted, and that it expected actions conformable to the friendship that exists between the two republics, guarantied by solemn treaties, and the assurances which that Government has given, the most recent and conclusive of which the undersigned takes the liberty to cite. When, on the 24th May of last year, Mr. Gorostiza, Mexican minister to that Government, on the subject of the proposition made to the Senate of the United Sates to acknowledge the independence of Texas, offered representations and objections which he wished to render valid, the Honorable Mr. John

Forsyth, Secretary of Foreign Affairs, stated, in his answer of the 29th of the same month, which is now under my eye. that he had received instructions from the President of the United States to assure him that the Government would adopt no resolution or decision on that question which was not founded on the same rules and principles which had guided it in the dissentions between Spain and her colonies þÿ that only when the parts should be well known, and not before, after a com- Saturday the 24th plete, impartial, and serious examination, and having always in view the considerations due to the friendly engagements that subsist between the two republics, the Government would then proceed to decide a question which, with the Mexican minister, is considered as of the greatest importance in its immediate effects and in its inevitable results. Such is precisely the language held by Mr. Secretary at the end of the month of May of last year, immediately afier the victory obtained by the insurgents. Has the case supposed by Mr. Forsyth now occurred? Arc the Texians in (he same position that the Mexicans were in repaid to Spain, when the United States acknowledged their independence ? Is there the slightest point of identity between a nation of more than six millions of inhabitants, who, by their sole eflorts, had thrown off the yoke of Spain, after a sanguinary struggle of eleven years, and without thousand vagabonds, without country, a few religion, without virtues, and without laws,

menaced by a numerous army, full of enthusiasm, marching to recover the laurels which a capricious destiny ravished at St. Jacinto? Shall the atrocious insult be offered to Mexico to suppose that it is incapable of vindicating her rights on the territory which those miserable adventurers have usurped, and shall she submit to the sneers of that republic ? If the undersigned should undertake to give a solution of these questions, he would render þÿ this note tedious by its length, and call in question the knowledge of the Secretary whom he has the honor to address. A document not less interesting than that just cited, is now under tiie eyes of the underdcrsigncd : I refer to the message of his Excellency General Jackson to the House of Retransmitting presentatives extracts on the 21st of last December, from the report of the agent whom he had despatched to collect information in relation to the situation, political and civil, of Texas, in consequence of the resolution of the two Houses, which declared that the independence ©1 Texas should be
acknowledged liv ibe United Stales in case they received satisfactory information of the existence of a Government capable of fulfilling the duties and obligations of an independent nation.

This official document, founded on the solid basis of justice and the law of nations, was published in t he American journals, as a new proof to Mexico of respect for her rights, its whole contents are interesting; it tends entirely to support a neutral position between Mexico and Texas. At the onset, in laying down general principles, it qualifies the act of acknowledging a new State as extremelydelicate, and attended by great responsibility ; it establishes that a premature acknowledgment, if not considered as a plausible hostile cause of war, may at least be regarded as proof of a hostile spirit towards one of the belligerent parties; it declares that every question relative to foreign nations was considered as seditious by the United States, and never credits them, but by most unquestionable evidence, not only for a final decision, but to guard its decisions from all imputation. Proceeding to particular cases, it recalls the prudence observed in the dissentions between Spain and her colonies, waiting not only till the ability of the new States was absolutely known, but also till all possibility of their being again subjugated bad disappeared. Recurring to Texas, it recounts the misfortune suffered at St. Jacinto, and its immediate consequences, and alludes to the resources that had been put in operation to repair it, and inclining to the opinion that the aeknowment of Texan independence ought to be postponed till the result of the expedition preparing to invade her should be known. But

why should the undersigned further fatigue the honorable Secretary by citing a document with which he is familiar, and which is at hand among the archives of his offiee ? It is sufficient to call to mind that the President, General Jackson, was of opinion at that time prudence dictated that the United States should wait, retaining their then attitude, till some one of the great foreign powers had acknowledged the independence of Texas, or at least till time and events proved, beyond doubt, that the inhabitants of Texas were able to sustain their sovereignty, and to support the Government which they had established. At this time, what events have occurred of so great importance as to induce the Government of the United States to depart from the circumspect and equitable line of conduct which bad been traced ? The Mexican Government is at a loss to know what guaranties have the Texans exhibited that are referred to in the message above cited? What evidence is there to justify an acknowledgment, particularly when we refer to the Consideration due to a neighboring and friendly Republic ? Assuredly none I The Mexican Government regards that of the Unitad States as too just to suppose that ignoble views of aggrandizement could govern its movements. Nevertheless, the measure complained of is incontestible ; it is announced in an official paper of the United States, the New Orleans Bee, and the undersigned has received instructions from his Excellency the President ad interim ol the Republic to

protest, as he does now protest in this solemn manner before all civilized nations, against the acknowledgment of the independence of the pretended Republic of Texas, made bv the United States of America, declaring that it cannot in any manner or mode, either now or at any time to come, weaken, diminish or compromit, in the least, the rights of of the Re- public of Mexico on the Territory Texas, nor the right which it possesses to employ all the means, which are or may be in its power to recover the said Territory.

The undersigned prays the honorable the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs of the United States to make known this note and protest to his Excellency the President of the United States, and takes this opportunity to offer him the expression of his respect and distinguished consideration. .'ose mabu ortjz monastemo.

St. Croix, CHRISTI A NSTED, ( MON DA Y ) June 12, 1837. TFb Aaue teen favored with the perusal of New York papers of the 18th May, received via St. Thomas. Nearly all ihe Banks in the United States had suspended specie payments ; and hud this measure have been adopted two months sooner, a great many failures wovld have been prevented. An order from the United Stales Treasury was received in New York on the 14 th May to require the payment of Custom house bonds for duties in specie. This caused great excitement in New York; the Collector of the Customs, Col. Swartout immediately started for Washington where he represented to the President and to the Secretary of the Treasury the impossibility of enforcing this order, mid that the merchants had it not in their power to pay in any other, but the Bank currency. The President and Secretary re' plied thai the laws were imperative, and that they possessed no option. Col. Swartout then declared that the laws were equally imperative On him, as on the President, but that lie would take the responsibility on himself of receiving Bank Bills in payment for Bonds, and this being acceeded to by the President, Col. Swartout returned immediately to New J ork, where he was received with acclamation by the merchants and people ; Mr. van Buren having previously issued a proclamation requiring the meeting of Congress on the first Monday of September. The New York Legislature have passed an act authorizing the suspension of Specie payments by the banks of the Stale of New York for one year. Business in New York was reviving in con-

sequence of this change in affairs, þÿ Stocks were rising, money getting plenty, and a prospect that Commercial affairs would soon resume their wonted activity. The state o f affairs between Mexico and the United States, continues very hostile ; þÿ Bus-, tamente has been elected President of Mexico, and it is said that Santa Anna was about embarking for Euiope.

She remained until the 10th, when a boat from the Mexican armed schr. Bravo came off to ascertain if any white lead was on board, but being answered in the negative, the boat returned on shore. On the 12th, a message was sent on shore by the U. S. sloop of war Natchez, demanding the release of the American schr. Champion, and if refused, the Mexican armed brig, formerly the Farmer, then at anchor off the Bar, should pay the forfeit, but the Commandant of the port returned answer that the Champion could not be released, ordered the officers of 'the boat on board with a message to the commander of the sloop of war to get under weigh and leave the coast immediately.

New Orleans May 4, 1837. Money Makket. þÿ There is no improvement in the money market. Nor can there be while such disastrous and gloomy news eternally assail our ears from New York. þÿ Auction on Monday the 2Gth instant at 12 Only think of the Canal Bank Stock in that city, down to 60 on the 27th ultimo ! All stocks are down. Here, they are a "dead weight." Money still commands out doors the "pound of flesh" Indoors nothing doing of consequence. Now and then a note for one or two thousand dollars creeps through the sanctum of some of our banks Even such facilities are grateful and serviceable to those who must have money. We repeat that the banks have it in their power to quiet the ears of capitalists and the community While they persist in their present course, the difficulties and alarm increase. It is true that their losses by the failure of the monopolists have been immense, and this is one cause why they are hampered. But they only add to the pressure occasioned by their losses and bad management when they act as individuals. They are money machines, and ought to be very cautious how they proclaim their own inability to benefit the public. But all arguments of this kind are thrown away upon these institutions Their rule is to expand in the hey-day of prosperity, till by their own folly they arc forced to contract, causing ruin to thousands. When well managed, however, they steer a middle course between these extremes.

Lady Scott. þÿ Lockhart gives the following description of Lady Scott in her youth : " Without the features of a regular beauty, she was rich in personal attractions ; a form that was fashioned as light as a fay's;' a complexion of the clearest and lightest olive ; eyes large, deep-set, and dazzling, of the finest Italian brown ; and a profusion of silken tresses, black as the raven's wing ; her address hovering between the reserve of a pretty young Englishman who has not mingled largely in general society, and a certain natural archness and gaiety that suited well with the accompaniment of a French accent. A lovelier vision, as all who remember her in the bloom of her days have assured me, could hardly have been imagined ; and from that hour the fate of the young poet was fixed."

The following is said to be one of the longest pauses on record: An old gentleman, riding over Putney Bridge, turned round to bis ser- vant, and said, " Do you like eggs, John ? ' " Yes, sir." Here the conversation ended. The same geutleman, riding over the same bridge that day twelvemonth, again turned round and said : " How V' " Poached, sir," was the answer.

A gallant old Scotch officer was narrating the unfortunate history of an early friend, who had been jilted by a fickle beauty of that age, in favour of the Duke A ;and be concluded the story thus, in a tone of much emotion, " Poor fellow, he never got over it : no, sir, it was the death of him and then, after a pause of much pathos, with a faltering voice, he added, " He did not live above fifteen years after it."

THE VIRTUE OF FRUGALITY. " We have been living in a period, and state of society, where the faculties of profit have been numerous beyond a parallel, and the frequent examples of sudden gain, flattering and seductive, temptations to cxtiavagance have increased daily. '1 housands have been spending upon anticipation, and dissipating, not hereditary wealth for of that we þÿ possessed þÿlittle not sure and tangible acquisitions, for those we have wanted patience to collect ; but that airy and invisible representative of wealth, credit, which, of all possessions, it is most necessary to economise and guard from violation. I he time seems to he approaching, it it has not alieady come, in which men are to learn, that they cannot, with impunity, despise the virtue of frugality ; and we have begun to see that uninterrupted profit is not the order of nature. We have found, that there are other enemies to rapid gains, besides the elements of nature, or the shoal which wrecks our vessels, or the indiscretion which mismanages our means, or the moth and rust which corrupt treasures long ago collected. Wo find that there may be serious obstructions to usual channels of profit, which check in an instant the movements of the vast machine of acquisition ; that the calculations of the aspiring man of business may be arrested, and every man in society comces of their prosperity, pelled to pause, some to others inquire into the sour- into the security of theif actual possessions. We find, that, in

the ordinary course of human affairs, changes occur, against which nothing but habitual frugality can provide ; and we arc taught to feci the importance of establishing the habits of a rising community in that state of moderate expense, which can be easily maintained through all these changes. It is a time, in fact, to learn the great riches ot frugality."

From the Barbadian, May 20. Having taken much interest in the novel undertaking, we have paid several visits to the Colonial Bank since its opening on the 15th instant, and find great pleasure and satisfaction in alluding to the encouraging circumstances under which it has commenced its important operations. We can state with truth that the gentlemen connected with the Institution have been very briskly employed ; the business, every day, appears to be as much as they can well get through. Receiving and paying pretty well occupies them. Fixed deposits, some to a considerable amount, have been invested. The Notes arc getting daily into circulation. People are beginning to appreciate the value of this Establishment, the usefulness of which to the community generally wc have never doubted, We feel it a duty to the Bank, as well as to the public, to remark

baits® T23'Jiwa>a3K aia®:iarcjiH&3 A/ris. on the great accomodation which is afforded by the Notes, which are so easy of carriage. The Bank, is well supplied with money with which to take up these Notes. By this means persons will be greatly accomodated with change when required The Bank will not give change for Doubloons ; but they will always give it for their Notes, in whatever money may be required. For instance, if one presents a five dollar Note he will receive, probably, three dollars in small change, and two silver dollars, or a two- dollai piece in gold. We trust, notwithstanding the obstacles thrown in the way of the circulation of the British Silver at the rate formerly established by the Proclamation of the Executive, which has been felt very much by all persons dealing with retailers, that there will be now no scarcity of other money change It would be as well, perhaps, if we were rid of the British Silver altogether, since no legal currency is permitted to be given to it. People are making a trade of it which is injurious to the public. The hucksters began it, and now some of the respectable mercantile houses will not receive it at the rate, 50 per Cent, which was supposed to be fixed by genei al consent at the public meeting. The sooner we have the old dollar coin and its fractional parts in circulation, alone, the better for the general convenience, especially if all accounts were kept in dollars and cents as at the Bank. The good working of the Colonial Bank, now commenced so auspiciously, will, we con-

fidently expect, facilitate all business operations and further the interests of every class in our very mixed and various community. We are authorised to state that the Notes of the Bank will be received currently at the Public Offices.

The present commercial difficulties in Liverpool, which have been greatly increased by the non-arrival of several American packets, not relieved by the arrival of two of these, which brought only more bills instead of specie, led on Thursday last to a meeting of influential merchants in the Liverpool Town Hall, at which it was determined to address a memorial to Government, praying for a loan of Exchequer hills to enable them to meet their engagements. This memorial was signed in the course of an hour and a half by 191 firms, the most respectable houses in Liverpool, and a deputation left that town with it on the following (Friday) morning for the metropolis þÿ Morning Post, April 10. The following is the memorial of the Liverpool merchants alluded to in the above meeting " to the right honorable the chancellor op his majesty's exchequer" " The Memorial of the undersigned Merchants, Brokers, and other inhabitants connected with the trade of Liverpool.

" Respectfully showeth þÿ That the distress of the mercantile interest is intense beyond example; and that it is rapidly extending to all ranks &l conditions of the community, so as to threaten irretrievable ruin in all directions, involving the prudent with the imprudent, tlio mannfactorer with the merchant, and the weavers, and labourers generally with the manufactorers themselves. " Your memorialists will not now enter on an examination of all the causes which have led to the existing convulsion ; they are aware that the late high prices of commodities mainly contribute to produce unfavorable exchanges. These high prices have passed, and are now succeeded by such a fall as cannot fail, in time, to attract the capital of the whole mercantile world to the relief of the present increasing pressure. " Your memorialists know better than to ask for any assistance which could restore high prices ; the losses must be borne. All they humbly ask is, that measure of relief which will save immense numbers, of all classes, from total ruin ; ruin not proceeding from insolvency, hut from the total impossibility of disposing of their property in time to meet their present and approaching engagements. " Your memorialists further submit that the present condition of affairs, unless mitigated, may involve the public peace and deeply affect his Majesty's revenue. " Your memorialists therefore pray that these premises may be taken into immediate consideration, and that such relief may be
granted as to your judgment may be deemed safe and expedient. " And your memorialists will ever pray."

Our intelligence from Grenada and Trinidad by the Southern mail is distressing. That shocking disease continues to spread in those islands ; in the former especially to a lamentable and fatal extent. The mortality is very great. It is not so severe in Trinidad- One shudders at the thought of this dreadful scourge reaching our island. The vigilance of the Quarantine, and Health Officers, is very much to be commended ; but again we call upon the Board of Health to establish a Rowguard in the Quarantine station at night We cannot he quite safe whilst that precaution is neglected. þÿy " '""' ' ",>_l j" ' - - .1 mm i From the Barbados Mercury, May 23, 183T- There is a prevailing opinion entertained, apparently amongst those who are considered good judges in such matters, that the present great scarcity of ground provisions and the consequent high prices, is owing chiefly to the system lately pursued by the agriculturists, of planting a much larger proportion of canes, & a much smaller in yams, potatoes, eddoes & the like, than formerly. If this really be the case, and of the fact we have not the slightest doubt, it is but poor policy, say to the least of it, as it must in the end lead to scarcity, if not want amongst the whole class of the labouring population, who, blow high low, or must have the allowance allotted them by law. þÿ Taking it for granted that the system followed in one which the planter considers more likely to yield a larger profit from the cultivation of his land, than under the old þÿone sugar being at present in demand both here and at home þÿ he may perhaps be, at the end of the year, a gainer. But on the other hand, if he does not raise ground produce enough to serve bis apprentices for the year, and is therefore compelled to buy if he can, there is a consideration by far more important than the accumulation of a few pounds, shillings, and pence, to be thrown into the scale, which will weigh heavily against it. In the first place, to depend upon a casual supply of food for the

the greatest disadvantage, the quantity daily to be given not in any way being dependant upon the price þÿ so that if one pound or a dozen pounds sell for a bit, the expense of feeding them would be proportionate ; and again, it is well known that nothing inspires that class with better spirits in performing their work, than the prospect being of well fed with their usual fare, the native products of the ground, such articles food, flour, rice, <xc., of as not at all suiting cither their wants or their appetites. Hence it may fairly be started as a question of some moment, whether the planter would be eventually a gainer by the present system of cultivation, it being plain that he must take part of his sugar money to buy provisions for his laborers, and should they be selling at a dear rate, it is well worth the calculation to ascertain if the net profits of an acre of land planted in canes would, under such circumstances, be more than, or equal to an acre planted in provisions, bearing in mind that from the former he can get only one crop per annum þÿ from the latter lie may obtain probably three or four of a different kind. þÿ But we must not, even with this view of the subject before us, throw all the blame of scarcity or dearness upon the planter, it being as much the fashion with the prmdial, who has his half acre allotted him in lieu of provisions, to plant it in canes, as it is with his employer. Now it is not only evident that a very great diminution in quantity must result from this

practice of the praedial, and consequently enhance the value of ground provision, but it is also quite clear that he must be dependent up- I on the market for a supply of daily food ; and how this is to be procured to any extent, it is not easy to discover, Another way in which the great scarcity of ground provision, especially yams, may be accounted for, is the great quantity annually exported to the neighbouring islands and colonies, and this being the case it is not really to be wondered at, if, in connection with the other causes assigned, we were obliged to pay treble the price for that and other equally necessary articles of food, both for ourselves and the laboring population. Upon this part of the subject, however, we will say but little.

a B From the Boston Daily Centinel and Gazette, May 25, 1837 IMPORTANT. proclamation from governor r1tner. Pennsylvania : In the name and by the authority of the L. S. Commonwealth of Pennsylvania : BY JOSEPH KITNEK, Governor of the said Commonwealth. A PROCLAMATION. Whereas, the genera! suspension of the payment of gold and silver, for their notes, by the banks of the country, presents a crisis in our pecuniary affairs, which demands the most serious consideration : And whereas, it has been represented to me by many citizens, that the Legislature should be convened at an early period, or that some other measures should be adopted to allay the uneasiness which pervades the public mind, and to obtain relief under the sudden embarrassment that has fallen upon us : Therefore, 1 have thought it right to issue this proclamation, for the purpose of declaring, among other things, that, upon mature deliberation, I have come to the conclusion that it is inexpedient for the present, to convoke the Legislature : Because the evils under which the good people of this Commonwealth labor, have not been produced by the action of the government of this state, but mainly by the unnecessary and unauthorised interference of the general government with the currency and rnonied transactions of the country ; and, therefore, the constituted authorities of Pennsylvania, cannot now, by any active measure, arrest or materially mitigate the misfortune, relief for which must come from the same source with the injury : Because all the measures which have been

proposed to be adopted by the State Legislature, to meet the emergency, would, in my opinion, rather increase, than diminish, the real difficulties of our condition. Authority to the banks to issue notes of denominations less than five dollars, would be the infliction of a great permanent evil, to alleviate a temporary embarrassment, and would only be the substitution of the lower denominations of a circulating medium for the higher denominations of the same, without withdrawing any of the .'alter from circulation, or giving to the one an\ stronger claims on public confidence than the other, thereby increasing the aggregate amount of bank notes, without increasing the amount of specie or property represented, and thus inevitably depreciating the actual value o! the existing representative currency. Die passage of a law to save th < forfeitures of the charters, to which the banks will become subject, by continuing to refuse specie for their notes, would only increase and render more lasting the mischief. The instant result would in all probability be a vast and ruinous increase of the bank note circulation þÿ a correspondent diminution of its real value þÿ dangerous a facility of obtaining bank leans þÿ a sudden rise in the nominal value of all kinds of þÿproperty a farther increase of the mad spirit of þÿspeculation and finally, the incurring of a real amount of debt, which must afterward be paid in hard money, dollar for dollar, to the ruin of thousands. The passage of a law for the stay of execu-
tion in case of debt, besides aggravating the evils just named, would accustom our citizens to a disregard for the obligation of law and for punctuality in their dealings, and would

beget a familiarity with the dependence of indebtedness, wholly inconsistent with the character of Pennsylvania citizens. For these reasons 1 deem it inexpedient for the present, to convene the Legislature. Ihe main object then of this proclamation is to address the patriotism, the good sense and interest of the citizens who direct the different banks of the Commonwealth. In their hands is placed, by this strange and sudden catastrophe, to a great extent, the present control of our prosperity. But fortunately for the community, the forfeiture or confirmation ot the charters of those institutions, will depend upon the estimate which public opinion, for the next six months, will form of tfie use which shall be made of the power that circumstances have thus given. If a reckless pursuit of profit, and a disregard of the welfare of society, should lead to a sudden and injurious increase of bank issues, the next meeting of the representatives of an injured community will undoubtedly visit the full penalty of the law on the faithless agents. If on the other hand an honest and patriotic application of the power now possessed by them, shall prevent the apprehended evils, and shall at the earliest possible period, restore the currency to its recently healthy condition, acts, under other circumstances unlawful, thus proved to have been compelled only by urgent necessity, and thus followed by no sinister perversion of power, will, beyond a doubt, be confirmed. To accomplish which desirable and just result, no

exertion will be spared by the executive at the proper time. In the mean time I shall take care, through the authority vested in the Auditor General, to keep the public and the Legislature, when it shall meet, informed of the amount of issues, and of the other transactions of the banks. If any bank should, after the suspension of specie payments, increase its amount of notes in circulation, it will be most important that the people's representatives, who will have before them the question of annulling or confirming the charter, should be aware of the fact. And, finally, it is the object of this proclamation, solemnly to call upon every citizen, in the name of his own and the public good, to sustain the honor and credit of the state and ol her institutions, at the present crisis. Let prudence and firmness be exerted by each in his own sphere, and there is no danger. þÿ The banks are believed to be abundantly able to meet all their liabilities. The only danger is to be found in rashness and excitement. It is evident that the present difficulty does not arise from any error in its management. The national government, with an unparalleled surplus of means, cannot pay its debts in the legal currency of the country. Our own state, with unfailing resources and increased facilities to promote and accommodate internal trade and business, is disappointed in her reasonable expectations of an in crease in the income of her public works over that of last year. Our farmers, mechanics, ma-

nufacturcrs 6c merchants, in the lull tide of profitable industry ifc entcrprize, are suddenly paralyzed in all their efforts. &the whole machinery of busy life stands still, without pestilence, death, or war, or the agency of any other great domestic or foreign calamity which usually produces such results. It must, therefore be that some error in the management of that currency built on mutual confidence, and which heretofore raised our country to unparalleled prosperity, has produced the present momentary stagnation. It will also be found that the intelligence and patriotism of American citizens will soon discover and apply the

remedy, and that the error wili soon be retrieved Nothing is required þÿ nothing is in the power of Pennsylvania but steady coolness during the emergency. The occasion will not be without its good effects, among which will be the opportunity presented to the next legislature to impose upon our banking system such guards and restrictions as present experience will point out for the benefit of the future. In the mean time, let the banks go on steadily, without oppressing their debtors, or seeking undue profit to themselves by increasing their notes in circulation ; and let a general and generous confidence in the solvency of the banks be cherished by the citizens, and all will be well. Given under m y hand and the great seal of the state, at Harrisburgh, the twentieth day of May, in the year of our Lord one thousand eight hundred and thirty-seven, and of the Commonwealth, the sixty- first. By the Governor. THOMAS H. BUUKOWES, Secretary of the Commonwealth.

Birth-Day of the Princess Victoria. We promised our readers some particulars of the Victoria Dinner, at the New York Albion Club on the 18th ult, but not having been able to collect them all in detail, we must content ourselves with the following sketch. At half-past five o'clock, the company, to the amount of forty or fifty, assembled at the Club House, and at six sat down to a very excellent repast. Dr. Bartlett having been called to the chair. Mr. Downing acted as the Vice President. Capt. Marryat, C. B. of the Roral Navy, the celebrated and highly popular writer, was present as a guest, and took his seat on the right of the chair. In reply to the toast þÿ "Captain Marryat " Peter Simple" arose England," and the Literature of and spoke to the follow- the author of ing effect : þÿ "Gentlemen, I assure you that it is with þÿ great pleasure that I find myself surrounded with so many of my countrymen, at such a distance from my native land ; and further that we are met together to celebrate an event of so much interest. " Y'our own gallantry will enable you fully to enter into my feelings, when 1 state to you that 1 have always conceived þÿ and 1 trust 1 may say so without being accused of disloyalty þÿ that I could serve a Queen with even greater zeal and fidelity than 1 could a King- Indeed, it would appear that women are more calculated to wield the sceptre than men ; for if we refer to our own history, we shall find that England never was so great and so glorious as under the dynasties of our Queens,

and that although they sometimes surrendered up their hearts to individuals, they always reserved their heads pro bono publico. Gentlemen, I have minutely investigated evety form of government at present existing, and have come to the conclusion that the most legiti- þÿ mate, the one most approaching to perfection and most agreeable to all parties, is a þÿ Petticoat Government. The advantages which would be derived from a youthful Queen being surrounded bv a youthful Ministry of her own sex, must be obvious. In the first place þÿ we should no longer hear an outcry against the cringing and servility of courtiers, for there could be no disgrace in bowing the knee to Youth and Beauty. It would be a great saving to the country þÿ for wcrc»any of us to solicit a pension from the fascinating Prime Minister, site would dismiss us more than contented with one of her sweetest miles þÿ and instead of taxing the people with the emoluments of a place, the lovely Chancellor of the Exchequer would satisfy the applicant bv assuring him that he already had a place in her affections. At present we snv the King can do no wrong þÿ and his Ministers alone are responsible. þÿ But if the Government wore constituted as 1 propose, no one would ever allow that either her Majesty her Ministers could do wrong or þÿ and here much grumbling would be saved to the country. A little intrigue will find its way into al| Governments, but I do not think that the spe. cics of intrigue to be expected in the one I re-

fer to, would be at all injurious to the Vonsti tution. Gentlemen, that there is a strong feeling towards this -form of Government in England, is made evident from the number of old women who holds offices under the Crown; but as I \ þÿ

v:»3tmwi3X ramomasma &xn perceive that you are already inflamed with the idea, and I do not wish to produce revo. lutionary feelings, I shall drop the subject For the honor you Itave done me by drinking my health, you have my thanks and gratitude. Allow me in return to have the pleasure of drinking yours, and to indulge the hope that some day or another we may talk over the hilarity of this meeting, when we shake hands in Old England, to whose future Queen our affections have this day been warmed, and whose natal day we have so joyously celebrated." This speech, and the novelty of the doctrine it enforced, were, as may be supposed, uncommonly well received. þÿ JSew- York Albion, June 3, 1837.

The Queen that is to be we mean, if she lives long enough, and no revolution shall de. prive her of the sceptre which of right is hers Princess Victoria, of whom we are writing, is at present in her 18th year ; site is in the bud of womanhood, and as beautiful to the eye as the full blown rose ; and the beauty of her person, we are told, is only excelled by the brilliancy of her mind, which she is ambitious still further to improve. The King, her uncle js so far advanced in years that it is more than probable the Princess will soon become the Queen of England, and wield the destinies of the triple thrones of England, .Scotland, and Ireland. Be it so þÿ for if all is true that is said, she has, as Napoleon said of one dear to him, " the head of a man upon the shoulders of a woman." Under these circumstances a smart young surgeon at Berlin stepped forward, and incognito to both( bv treating his subject to suit their different tastes, succeeded in assuring the doctors of Riga that homoeopathy was not a system of quackery, and of convincing those of St. Petersburg that it was As the candidate, essays were anonymous, and very little direct intern ource between the two societies it was of course not known that the favorite reasoner cut with a two-edged sword; but now that the discovery lias been made, it has subjected those learned doctors to very gene, ral banter throughout Germany. We are sorry to learn, by the following communication, that the Act for establishing the Local Bank of Jamaica, passed in last Sessions ol the Island Legislature, has been disallowed by His Majesty's Ministers. We call upon all classes of our fellow colonists to view this case calmly and deliberately ; and to say how far they can consider it to correspond with Mr. M 'Queen's professions of disinterestedness towards ourselves on the part of the Mammoth monopolists in London : to promote whose views and interests he came to this island the paid agent ; for there can be little doubt that this step was advised through the impure and selfish influence of the Colonial Bank proprietors, who could not endure a competition, even in the traffic "of dollars of acknowledged weight and fineness.'1 We. however, hope that the inhabitants of this Island will, with one voice, call meetings in every parish to express their spontaneous and unqualified indignation at the unjust and unmerited contempt, with which, all their acts to meliorate the condition of this country and its inhabitants arc received by his Majesty's Ministers. If the Colonial Bank was intended to be of benefit to this Country, as well as to its London proprietors ; why should not the people resident in the Island enjoy at least a portion of those privileges, conceded to the former, at our expense ? Or are we, who are chiefly in-

terested in the prosperity of the Country, and considered " Aliens," as Lord Lvndhurst its preservation for the British Crown, to he would say. Are we alone þÿ our rights; our properties ; and our feelings, to he sacrificed to satiate the rapacity of any set of speculating money mongers, possessing no common ties of interest or sympathy with us? We suppose the next step the Ministry will take, will be to disallow any act which our Legislature may deem it their duty to pa-s, for promoting Steam Navigation or Rail Roads. þÿ St. Christopher Adv. From the New York Express, May 20. (From the National Gazette.) We present to our readers to day, a third letter to Mr Adams, from the President of the Bank of the United States, which will be read with not less interest and advantage than the preceding ones. It is a perfectly clear and satisfactory exposition of the existing state of things, and cannot fail to carry conviction to the minds of all. It shows that the course adopted by the banks of I'hilapelphia, was imperatively demanded by circumstances beyond their control, and that it will be most conducive to the ultimate benefit of the community and country þÿ that the Bank of the United States has been actuated in this measure by the same spirit of patriotism and wisdom which has guided all its proceedings, and that it will be ready at a moment's warning to do its part in restoring matters to their former condition of peace and prosperity. Philadelphia, May 13, 1837. My Dear Sir þÿ You were good enough to express a wish to know my own views of the present state of things, and I hasten to give them without reserve. You may perhaps remember that in my letter to you of the Uth November last I stated what seemed the real causes of the embarrassments then existing, and the appropriate remedies for them, adding that bv their adoption " confidence would be restored in many days twenty-four " hours, six months and repose farther at experience least in as has only confirmed that opinion. I believe now, as I believed then, that the events of this week might have been readily prevented þÿ

and that the unhappy perseverance in the measures then deprecated, has reduced the country to its present condition But 1 have no leisure now to discuss the subject, and no disposition to indulge in unavailing regrets It will be more profitable to look distinctly at tne present condition of the banks and the country, and to suggest their respective duties to themselves and to each other. All the deposit banks of the Government of the United States in the city of New York suspended specie payments this week ; the deposit banks elsewhere have followed their example ; which was of course adopted by the State banks not connected with the Government. I say of course, because it is certain that when the Government banks cease to pay specie, all the other banks must cease, and for this clear reason. The great creditor of the United States is the Government. It receives for duties the notes of the various banks, which are placed for collection in certain Government banks, and arc paid to those Government banks in specie if requested. Now if these government banks, the depositories of the public revenue, will not pay specie, for the veiy warrants drawn upon them by the Treasury þÿ the government of the United States from that moment ceases to pay specie to the citizens of the United Stales. As moreover the government receives for duties only specie and the notes of specie-paying banks, the instant its own doposite banks cease to pay specie, the government must refuse to receive the notes of its own doposite banks,

and can receive no notes except those of banks not deposite banks. On the one hand then, the government is bound to pay its debts in specie, and it lias no means of procuring specie except from the banks not connected with the treasury, so that these banks find all their notes collected and paid into the treasury for duties, converted immediately into specie

iD&SJSlfc TS&STSStJMSK. ttlSQSSR&SrM A%TX for the use of the government þÿ while the deposite banks will not pay their debts to the other banks in specie, nor pay the treasury warrants in specie Take for instance this example. The claimant under the French indemnity had certain monies due him in France The government imported it in gold for him and when the day of distribution ar- þÿ rived, he obtained an order for his portion. þÿ But instead of receiving his own share of his own proper identical gold, he has received neither gold nor silver, but the notes of the deposite banks which very notes the govern- þÿ ment itself would refuse to receive from this verv claimant, lor any debt which he might owe to the government So long, therefore, as the government and the government banks will not pay specie to other banks, it would be rashness in those banks to pay specie to them, and as they cannot make a discrimation in those whom they will pay, the only alternative is to concur with the government banks in the general suspension. Our Philadelphia banks saw this. They thought it useless to carry on so unequal an intercourse, in which they were to pay to New \ork, while Now York refused to pay to Tennsylvania, for if the Pennsylvania banks paid while those of New York did not, the whole revenue would have been turned into Pennsylvania notes and specie demanded. In the midst of these disorders, the Bank of the United States occupies a peculiar position, and has special duties Had it consulted merely its own strength, it would have con-

tinued its payments without reserve. But 1st. Like all the other Pennsylvania banks, it owed a duty to the citizens of our own state ; and it was not disposed to stand aloof from a general movement of the other state institutions, which however it might regret, it could not censure. þÿ 2d. It was not inclined, moreover, to discredit, by a refusal to receive it, the paper of the other state banks which had ceased to pay specie, still less to force its Pennsylvania debtors to pay their debts in specie, when other citizens in other states were allowed to pay in a less costly medium ; thus breaking down for the benefit of other states, the merchants and manufacturers and mechanics of Pennsylvania. 3d. While the vaults of all the other banks were closed, the government of the United States would have no resource to procure specie," but the Bank of the United Stales, which ought not to assume the risk of being the only source of supply for bullion to the government and the land offices, as well as for exportation. 4th The deposit banks of the government would not pay their debts to the Bank of the United States. Why then should the Bank of the United States pay to these institutions, on account of the government, specie for their notes, wftcn these very banks would not pay their own debts? There would have been an equal want of reciprocity and of justice in such a proceeding. 5th. There was another reason against it, final and decisive. From the moment that the deposite banks of New York failed to

comply with their engagements, it was manifest that all the other deposit banks must do the same, that there must be a universal suspension throughout the country, and that the treasury itself, in the midst of its nominal abundance, must be practically bankrupt. In such a state of things, the first consideration is, how to escape from it þÿ how to provide .at the earliest practicable moment, to change a condition which should not be tole-

rated beyond the necessity which commaml ed it. The old associations, the extensive connections, the established credit, the large capital of the Bank of the United States, render it the natural rallying point of the country for the resumption of specie payments þÿ It seemed wiser, therefore, not to waste its strength in a struggle which might be doubtful, while the Executive persevered in its present policy, but to husband all its resources, so as to profit by the first favorable moment, to take the lead in the early resumption of the United specie payments. Accordingly the Bank þÿ States assumes that position. of From this moment, its efforts will be to keep itself strong, and to make itself þÿstronger always prepared and always anxious to assist in recalling the currency and the exchanges of the country to the point from which they have fallen. It will co-operate cordially and zealously with the government, with the government banks, with all the other banks, and with any other influences which can aid in that object. In the mean time, two great duties devolve on the banks and the country. The first regards foreign nations þÿ the second our own. We owe a debt to foreigners, by no means large for our resources, but disproportioncd to our present means of payment. We must take care that this late measure shall not seem to be an effort to avoid the payment of our honest debts to them. \\ e have worn, and eaten, and drunk, the produce of their industry þÿ too much of all, perhaps,

but that is our fault, not theirs. We may take less hereafter, but the country is dishonoured unless we discharge that debt to the uttermost farthing. The second duty is to ourselves. We should bear constantly in mind, that the step which has been taken is excusable only on the ground of an overruling necessity. We must not make the remedy itself a disease. It must not be the pretext of extravagant loans or issues These arc already sufficiently inflated, and if we have voluntarily removed the most familiar and established check upon all issues þÿ their immediate convertibility into coin it is our duty to substitute some effectu- þÿ al restraints, which may enable us to restore the currency without delay or difficulty to a safe and wholsomc condition. 'I he result of the whole is, that a great disaster has befallen the country. Its existence thus fur is only a misfortune, its continuance will be a reproach, from which all true men must rally to save her. We must try to render it as short as possible, waiting patiently and calmly for the action of the government, and in the mean time diminishing its dangers by great prudence and forbearance. For myself, you know how zealously 1 have labored to avert this misfortune. With not less anxiety 1 shall now strive to repair it. With great respect and regard, yours, N. BIUDI.E. Hon. J. Q.. Adams, Quincy, Mass. þÿ þÿ »" Front the New York Express, May 27.

New Orleans, May 17 þÿ We have below, from the New Orleans Bee, more frightful details of the awful and wholesale butchery of one hundred and seventy five human brings, who have fallen victims to a steamboat captain. The apathy of the people of this country upon all subjects that regard human life, is ore of the most singular traits in the American character þÿ for in no other land, not even where armies arc slaughtered by thousands,

BA5ISIK. could such butcheries as this be perpetrated with impunity. Congress has in vain attempted action, but the people felt no interest in the matter, and yet our friends, our brothers, our sisters, those whom we love as we love ourselves, are at the mercy of such a butcher as the captain of this steamer. If he had murdered a single man, the law would hang. Now that he ought to be hung one hundred and seventy-five times, he will anon be the captain of another boat, with the power to murder as many more. ADDITIONAL PARTICULARS OF THE LOSS OF THE REN SHERROD. The Natchez papers contain further particulars of the deplorable loss of the Hen Sherrod. At the time she took lire, she was engaged in a race with the steamer Prairie ; and the fire took front the great heat of the boilers, caused by raising her steam to its extreme power, þÿ a barrel of whiskey was placed on deck for the use of the hands during the race, who drank to excess and became intoxicated. At about 12 o'clock at night the furnace became so heated that it communicated fire to the wood, of which there was on board about sixty cords. When the crew dicovered the fire, they all left their posts and ran for the yawl without giving any alarm to the passengers, who were all asleep in their births The captain for a time attempted to allay the extreme confusion by stating that the fire was extinguished; twice he forbid the lowering of the yawl, which was attempted by the deck hands and passengers. the shrieks ol nearly

three hundred persons on board now rose wild and dreadful. The cry was to the shore ! to the shore! and the boat made for the starboard shore, but did not gain it, as the wheel rope might have given way, or the pilot been driven by the tlames from his station. 1 he steam was not let oil, and the boat kept on. The scene of horror now beggared all description. The yawl, which had been filled with the crew, had sunk, drowning some who were in it, and the passengers had no other alternative than to jump overboard without taking even time to dress There were ten ladies on board, who all went overboard without uttering a single scream, some drowning instantly, and others cling+ng to planks þÿ two of the number were finally saved. The steamboat Alton arrived half an hour after the Columbus, but from the carelessness or indiscretion of those on board, was the means ot drowning many persons floating in the water. She drove into the midst of the exhausted sutlcrers, who were too weak longer to make exertion, and by the commotion occa-
sioned by her wheels, drowned a large number. A gentleman by the name of Hamilton, from Limestone county, Alabama, was floating on a barrel, and sustaining also a lady, when the
the lady was drowned, but Mr. Hamilton canto up and Routed down the river fifteen

mifc&OMEWS AT33 lj miles; when he was taken up by the steamei Statesman. Such have been the improvements in surgery, that there are some hopes that a cure for consumption may at length be effected by its aid. It is a line in which no efforts have as yet been made with a view to the absolute alleviation of this all pervading disease. The attention of medical men has never been directed to so apparently hopeless a resource as a means of arresting the career of a malady hitherto regarded as exclusively within the province of the physician, and not having even a remote bearing to the remediate virtues residing in the knife. But such will probably be the turn which things will take, and under this conviction I am induced to lay before the

unhappily, too common disorder. In order to render this matter intelligible to the mass of people who are most deeply interested in the discovery, it will be necessary to make them, in a measure, acquainted with the opinions which have been hitherto entertained by physicians in regard to the nature of this disease, and to give a brief description of the structure of the lungs, and the manner in which they effect the vital function of oxidizing the blood. The lungs are bodies of a loose or spongy consistence, contained within the chest. They are placed in the right and left sides, and are separated from each other by a membranous partition, running from under the breastbone directly to the back-bone. The lung of the left side is the smaller, from the heart being situated in that cavity. The windpipe goes down the neck, and dividing into two branches, enters into the back part of the lungs close upon the spine. The lungs lie loose in the chest, like a bag or bladder, whose orifice is at the windpipe. þÿ We will suppose it to be a bladder inside of a bellows þÿ if we stop up the hole or valve in the bottom board of the bellows, and suppose the mouth of the bladder to come out at the nose, it is then in precisely the same circumstances that the lungs are within the chest, Raise the handles, and the air passes in at the nose and fills the bladder inside the bellows þÿ depress the handles, and the bladder is emptied. But let us open the valve underneath the bellows, and the air, when the handles are elevated,

will rush into this opening, instead of the smal. Icr orifice of the nose. The lungs are in the same relative situation. Make an opening in the inside of the chest, and when the ribs are raised in the act of breathing, tho air is drawn through this new passage in prelcrence to passing bv the more circuitous way of the mouth and windpipe. As the air is drawn in upon the exterior surface of the lung, the latter (which we will suppose the bladder again) is pressed down and more and more emptied by every breath, until it is reduced to its smal. lest size, and all the cavity outside of it is filled with air. The lung (for these arc cases which are not speculative, but of almost daily occurrence) is compressed in this manner to a body not larger than the first þÿ which shows the exceeding sponginess of its structure. This opening has sometimes been made by accident, sometimes to give issue to matter or air collected within the cavity, and for various other purposes. It is- practicable as a curative means only, from the fact that the lungs arc contained in two separate and distinct apartments, divi-
