It they were both in one cavity, and the air were let in upon their outside, there would be an end to life, as no breath could gain admit" tance to the inside of the lungs. But as it has been proved in numerous instances of disease, and where operations diave been performed' that a person can live by the breath of one lung, and allow the other to lie idle, the idea originated of attempting to cure a disease in the one dung, which is under your mastery while the other goes on with its functions. þÿ The only way in which consumption is ever cured, is by the collapsing or drying tip of the lungs, the cessation of breathing in it, and the sinking of that side of the chest The other side of the chest generally becomes enlarged. Consumptive people live on for years, when to all intents and purposes, they have not half public the following plan for the cure of this a lung. And a distinguished writer has ex' pressed the opinion that one twentieth part of the air usually taken into the lungs at one respiration, is sufficient to sustain life. The system of cure here proposed is founded on a careful consideration of these facts. If the lung can be placed at rest by the admission of air to the cavity of the chest, the great obstacle to the cure of consumption is removed So long as it is kept continually in motion by the passage of the air through every portion ol it, an ulcer or any other disease which may exist cannot possibly heal. If the motion did

not aggravate the complaint, the state of distention in which the lungs is kept and the separation of the diseased or ulcerated surfaces maintained by this distension, would prevent the union of the opposite sides of the ulcers. A wound w ill not unite unless the edges are kept together þÿ and a sword wound of the lung is only cured bv the instantaneous sinking down of the wounded organ and the consequent contact which is produced between the sides of the cut. Thus nature seems to have pointed out this means of cure, and to have placed consumption, as it were, under an impossibility of being removed by medicinal remedies, or by any other means than the knife. It is like the hip complaint in this respect. It is impossible to produce a perfect state of lest in that joint þÿ as in any position in which the patient may be placed, silting, standing, or lying, every movement of the body centres in the head of the thigh bone, and continually aggiavates the existing disease and renders it incurable. Now, the object of the operation for consumption. is to make a permanent opening into the side of the chest, so as to allow the air to enter freely and compress the þÿlung give to nature an opportunity (while the lung is in a state of rest) to absorb the diseased matter, or to heal the ulcerated parts by cicatrization, and to afford the surgeon an opportunity to tesort to the ligature or knife, where they may be benclicial. In the first place, the surface on which nature has to act in her cura-

tive attempts, is very much reduced ; in the next place, there is no interruption to her efforts, occasioned by the process of breathing, or by the irritation of the hectic fever, which seems to be simply an indication of her struggles and her inability to conquer a great disþÿease sincewe invariably see it manifested when the body is labouring under a very extensive external sore, or an internal disease or abscess where there is no possible chance for the escape of the matter or the consolidation of the parts, as in the ease of the liver and tho lungs In the next place, the matter, or pus, instead of compelling the lungs to violent efforts for its expulsion through the wind"

pipe, and the want of strength to do which is frequently, if not generally, the immediate cause of death in this disease, finds a ready issue by the artificial opening. Again the parts cannot so well become callous in a state of quiescence, and if they have already become so bv " the constant motion, as in fistula the compression to which they arc subjected will promote their union, as in ulcers on the eg þÿ their collapse alone favors this result. þÿ To be brief, where applications, incisions, inspections, &c. are required, they are easily made. If it is lound necessary to remove any diseased part, it can be effected. It is not necessary to enter into the details of the operation. It is not as severe as one half of those daily performed in this city ; and as to its practicability, we will not throw away reasons in discussing a matter which admits of no dispute. Those who are aware that an incesion had been made in the abdomen, and an ovarium of enormous size successfully reremoved, (by Dr. 1) I, þÿRogers,) that the bold and skilful hand of Dr. Aiott has entered the breast and almost passed a ligature around the heart þÿitself those who know that hipe joints have been made by a dash of the knife, as in a ease by Dr. J. Kearny Rogers þÿ will not wonder that a diseased lung which has censed to perform its functions, should be seized and þÿ taken out mainly from its location in the body much less need they be alarmed at the trival operatidn of making a small incision in the side as the first step in the way of giving life

to the destined victim of consumption. Were the operation the most terrible, as it is the most trifling, there would be no cause for apprehension that a man's system in so low a state as that of a consumptive patient would not be able to bear the shock. Persons reduced to the very confines of the grave by any long protiactcd disease in one of the extremities, undergo amputation better, and rise with renovated health from its effects sooner, than those who are brought down in the full strength of their bodily powers, and are compelled to submit to a mullilation of one their members. þÿ The danger ol the operation is less, the pain is less, in proportion to the lownessof health and strength of the patient. Instead of giving stimulants to sustain the system, we should in many cases rather Im'e recourse to bleeding, in order to diminish the quaniu of blood circulating through the lungs. Without, therefore, particularising the different steps of the operation in these preliminary observations, we shall content ourselves with presenting a summary of the arguments which have been advanced in favour of the success of these remediate measures for tho effectual cure of consumption, and leave readers to judge of the degree of confidence to of flattering, against nty ow n conviction, guilty which they are entitled. 1 would not be that delusisn and fallacy of anticipation which are often observed among consumptive subjects, and which frequently lead them to hope, in defiance of all the evidences of approaching

dissolution, that they arc at that vcrv time on the point of perfect restoration to he'ulth, and to hold up their shrivelled arm to you and ask you to took at the plumpness of it as an incontrovertible proof of their returning vigour. Much hallucinations arc too melancholy to he trilled with in so grave a manner. The reasons upon which I found my assurance of tho feasibility of this mode of cure, are : health First, with a man can breathe and retain his one of his lungs only. good Secondly, nature sometimes effects a cure by drying up one of the lungs, and this is the only method in which she ever docs effect a cure. Thirdly, the operation is neither difficult nor dangerous. And fourthly, the diseased lung may be wholly moved if necessary. L. I1. N. M. ROTHSCHILD. The following remarks on this eminent capitalist occur in a pamphlet on the Currency and Joint Stock Banks, just published, by D. Solomons : þÿ " An event of some importance, in connexion with the derangement of the circulation of the country, and which appears to have escaped observation, is the death of the late N. Al. Rothschild. It is well known with what dexterity that eminent individual managed the exchanges ; how he prided himself 111 distributing his immense resources, so that no operation of his own should abstract for a lengthened period the bullion from the Bank of England ; and although it may be urged he kept the exchanges in an artificial state, and therefore produced no ultimate good, yet the sudden withdrawal of this artificial aid in ail opportune moment, has tended to aggravate evils, which his energy and promptitude might have checked. The difficulties which have been experienced since his death, induce mc to think, that no one ever displayed greater ability than he did in equalizing the exchanges, and 1 attribute much of the late embarrassment to the loss of that activity, zeal and enterprise, which lie always displayed in times of financial difficulty ; and although the operations of his important house are continued, it is impossible at once to replace that moral influence which the acknowledged good judgment of the head of that opulent firm had established for himself, not only in Great Britain, but throughout the whole of the commer-
cial world.''

From the New York Express, May 27. from the european correspondent of the new york daily express. o. p. q. no. 55. tfie commercial crisis in france To the Editor of the New York Daily Express. Paris, March 21st, 1837. Gentlemf.n þÿ There is a commercial crisis in France. We most examine its character, and its origin, its immediate consequences þÿ and its probable results, '1 his crisis is severe þÿ i9 becoming worse every day þÿ is extending from the capital to the provinces þÿ and is reacting again from the provinces on Paris. 1 his crisis is unlike those of America or of Great Britain, They are not of a political character þÿ they are purely commercial or financial. Sometimes they arise from an excess of speculation þÿ sometimes from a tampering with the þÿcurrency sometimes from absurd laws and regulations as to the circulating medium þÿ sometimes from very bad harvests and a þÿdearth and sometimes from war, and the suspension of foreign commerce. All the crisis of a commercial character both in Great Britain and the United States, which have taken place during the last twenty-five years, may be traced to one or other of these causes, or to their combination. Such is not the character of the commercial crisis in France. Its origin is of a different þÿkind and it is necessary that I should go at some length into the circumstances which have produced it. Before however I look to its origin, let me enter into some explanations as to the extent, degree and precise character of this crisis. þÿ The Funds have fallen! The -Savings Banks

are run upon ! Failures are four times more numerous than they ever are at this period of the year. Twenty five thousand workmen at Lyons are out of employ. Ten thousand workmen at St. Etienne are in a similar condition. The laboring portions of the populations at Rouen, Havre, and in various other towns and cities are in want of bread and work. The journeymen Cabinet makers, Upholsterers, Carpenters, Dyers, Weavers, and other artizans of Paris are suffering extremely, and the masters have been obliged to discharge a large portion of their men. Besides this, Bills of Exchange are not paid þÿ renewals are sought for þÿ second rate, though good paper, cannot be discounted at all þÿ and even first rate paper is not discounted under 5 per cent. Money is very scarce. The wholesale dealer does not give his usual spring orders to the manufacturer. The shopkeeper docs not purchase of the wholesale dealer. The keepers. There is a general " malaise No public do not throng the shops of the shop- ." one branch of manufactures, trade or commerce is prospering. There is a general stagnation. The taxes arc in arrears. The rents due 15th January are not yet þÿpaid and we are only a month of the next quarter day. Some trades are so bad, that is doing. Some manufacturers, as in the silk and cotton trades, have stopped manufacturing þÿaltogether and the mayors of Lyons, St. Ltienne, and other places, have come to Paris, to know what is to be done In France, the Government is always first applied to. In

England, they hold public meetings, open subscriptions, and each one puts his shoulders to the wheel ; and so the machine is impelled forwards; but in I' ranee nothing of this takes þÿplace and the first application, is always made to the Government ! The crisis is so severe in Paris, that even the consumption of

Tas'jpjiTxcjsx aaajmi &3 meat and bread, and wine and vegetables is diminished. The markets of Secaux, of Poissy, Bercy, and all other places from which Paris is supplied with provisions, are so overstocked, that the farmers and graziers, gardeners and wine merchants can hardly comprehend what it all means for the crisis must be severe indeed, when the French begin to economize in dress or diet. We have had also some very extensive failures, stoppages, and suspensions of payment, and all men in business, whose fortunes are not colossal, have been more or less annoyed þÿ more or less pinched. I have entered into these particulars, in order to shew you, that this is a real crisis þÿ and in order that you may be prepared for insurrections and emeutes should they follow ; for the French population have no sort of notion of suffering peaceably and quietly when a crisis continues for any length of time. At Amiens we have had troubles al ready. But they have not lasted long. Let me now explain to you the " origin" of this deplorable state of things, for by doing this you will understand in the first place why we are suffering þÿ and, secondly, how long we are likely to do so, viz , until the causes of this misery shall be removed. The origin of all this commercial misery and stagnation, depreciation of public and private credit, and stoppage of trade and commerce, is uncertainty. The French are ' uncertain' as to the durability their of government. What is the consequence ? Why, lands remain uncultivated, houses unsold, and

building ground undisposed of. The manufacturer will not engage in any new speculalion þÿ the banker will not lend money at long dates þÿ the capitalist will not advance funds, I them from even for promising undertakings The most brilliant prospects will not tempt the monicd man. He is afraid of losing all. He sees nothing Jike stability in the government. He argues that he is sure of nothing which is out of his own hands: and he asks, " If the government be overthrown to- morrow, what i enlist themselves þÿ would become of my securities /" Now this uncertainty as to be durability of a govern- ! merit, is an immense evil. There cannot be a greater one for commerce. From the moment monied men and bankers and manufacturers and merchants, feel that the ground beneath their feet is trembling, and that a political earthquake may swallow them up, how can you expect therr to give credit? þÿ without credit and confidence, there can be no ! proposed and yet commerce. It is not that money is wanted in France, or that the precious metals are scarce. It is not that a plague has decimated the population, or that any vast change has come over the spirit, habits, or customs and modes of life of the people. No, nothing has occurred ; and yet we have a commercial crisis þÿ But why have not the merchants, manufacturers, bankers and capitalists of France any confidence in the durability of the Govern- i Duke dc Nemours. ment? Is it because Meunicrand Champion, Alibaud and Fieschi have attempted to take

liteially nothing away the life of the king? No; for what, after all, would it matter in England , where the Government of a Representative and limitted Monarchy is stable, if the king should die, or even be murdered? All good men would weep over such an event as þÿregicide and all wise men would deplore it ; þÿ but in England, no sooner would the hands of the assassin have put an end to the life of the þÿking than the people would raise to the throne his neicc " Victoria," as his successor. " The King is dead? þÿ hong live "the young Queen!" would be uttered in the same breath ; and millions of British subjects would reply "yes

A'OS. þÿ long live the young Queen !" Now, I am neither praising, nor blaming this. I am stating a fact þÿ a mere fact þÿ but a fact quite undeniable and important. And why is not this the case in France? Some will tell you, because in France the New Dynasty has only been formed since 1830, whereas in England it has existed since 1088. But this is no reason. It the New dynasty were popular þÿ were national þÿ were loved and confided in by the people, the mere circumstance of its youth would be no argument against it. Just the reverse ! It would be petted as a darling child þÿ and loved the more tenderly, for its youth and origin. It would have no arrears against it of laults þÿ No past errors of former kings atone for; and its virgin freshness, to would ever be an argument in its favor. The fact is, that the faults of the Government since 1831 have been so numerous, so flagrant, and so sad þÿ that even those who have encouraged that Government in all its mistakes and errors now perceive that the people stand aloof from it þÿ that there is no union between the people and the Government they þÿinstituted and that as the people do not sanction the present arrangement, there can be no stability about it. I will give you a few specimens of the reasons which have led to this conviction. The National Guards no longer perform their duties with pleasure or alacrity. This is a fact. A law is passing to make what was once a voluntary and agreeable service, a compulsory one. How is this? There

was a time when the National Guards of I'aris flocked by tens of thousands to the Champe de Mars. They flock no longer Every sort of excuse is made by the Paris citizens to save serving. The law now passing, is a most unpopular law. It is to enmpe/t all to serve. It is to compell all to clothe themselves in an uniform, for which multitudes are unprepared to pay. It is to subject to fines and imprisonment, all who do not þÿserve who do not. voluntarily and who do not do their duty and mount guard when required. In this compulsory service the inhabitants of Paris only see an evidence of the unpopularity of the government, and that unpopularity is to them an evidence of its non-durability. Take another example. The Journal called the " Charivari," has lately been tried for having written a violent article against the apanage of the Duke de Nemours 1 It has been so tried before the Court of Assizes of the Seine þÿ It was acquitted. Why we. it acquitted Because the Jury, composed of ? respectable men, and citizens who, from tie r position in life, must love order, and yet who wished to show to the government that the þÿJury i. e., the Electors and National Guards of the Department of the þÿSeine were, and arc most adverse to this income taw of the

This verdict of guilty against the Government, and of not guilty against the Journal, hastened very much indeed to open the eves of the merchants, bankers, and manufacturers, to the instability, because of the unpopularitv, of the present Government. Take a third example The uncertainty þÿa to the fate of Algiers has done a great deal towards Increasing the commercial crisis. A great quantity ol manufactured goods were so manufactured on the ground of the conviction that they would be required for the new French colony of Algiers. That conviction is now destroyed. I he defeat at Constantino þÿ the turning out ol Clauscl from his post of Governor of þÿAlgiers the declarations of Al. Dupin

and his friends against the colonization of the north of þÿAfrica and the uncertainty as to what will be the decision of the Chamber of Deputies with reference to the þÿcolony have made the merchants decline, making further speculative purchases, until it shall first be known what the Government will do with the colony, and what will be the fate of those who have already embarked their money in the enterprise. Take a fourth example. The government is quarrelling with the army. This is known to all France. Not only is the government quarrelling with the National Guards, but it is quarrelling also with the army. Gen. Voiral has been displaced from his command at Strasbourg. Marshal Clausel has been turned out at Algiers. Gen Schramen, who was most popular with the army, has been displaced of Paris, for simply approving as a deputy at Alsace a petition presented for the re- integration of Gen. Voiral. The officers and subofficers of the 62d Legion at Algiers, have been turned out of the army, because they signed a protest against the report of Marshal Clausel, accusing them of cowardice ; and now we are told that the whole regiment has risen in favor of its officers and sub-officers This complicated quarrel of the army and the government is naturally calculated to excite 110 strong belief in the durability of the government. Take another example 1 The rejection of the law oj disjunction by the majority of the Chamber of Deputies, has proved to the monied interests, that even the Chamber cannot be lolly

relied on in supporting that government. þÿ The chamber was said to be decidedly ministerial. M. Guizot felt so sure of his law of disjunction, it. The monied interests were told, The that he would not even plead for " Minister may rely on the Chamber of I)epu. ties." They were deceived þÿ and they now feel no confidence in the Chambers. 1 hey were certain " " of the majority, they said, the very day on which the bill was þÿrejected and now they are all uncertainty." " Take another example 1 The laws as presented by the ministers for a marriage portion for the Queen of the þÿBelgians for an income for the Duke de Nemours þÿ for two millions extra secret service money, .and for punishing the crime of "non-revelation" of plots against the Government, will not pass in the form and to the extent presented by the Government. They have all been so much amended by the Commissions of the Chambers to which they have been referred, that, with the exception of" the marriage portion law for the Queen ol lie Belgians, they can scarcely be recognised as the same measures ; and even, though so altered and modified, it is still doubtful if these laws will pass. The probable rejection, or at any rate total change, of these measures, has of course not at all tended to convince the monied interests that the Government per- is manent ; and in this state of uncertainty they refuse both to spend and to lend. And when you add to all this, 1st, tire progress of republicanism in the army ; 2d, the increase of the

number and sale of the opposition prints ; .'ldi the existence of secret societies ; 4th, the increase of regicidal attempts against the life of the King ; 5th, the non-conviction of journals for manifest libels on the Government ; Oth, the union of such men as Dupin and Barrot, and of Ganneron and Manguin, against the ministers of the King; 7th, the weakening, if not nearly the destruction, of the alliance between France and England ; tub, the defeat

vsstciritfss ikbweb&i&qs aths of the Christinos in Spain, and the probable triumph of Don Carlos ; 9th, the approaching death of the King of Prussia, and the warlike and ultra-monarchical views of the Prince Itoyal ; 10th, the hostile attitude of Uussia and Great Britain towards each other; 11th, the bad state of affairs in Portugal ; and 12th, the progress of democracy all over Europe, þÿ you cannot be astonished that great uncertain, ty should be felt as to the duration of the French Government. Well, then, it is this uncertainty which is the cause of the present commercial crisis in France. It is of course aggravated by the financial embarassments of the money markets of the United States, and by the uncertainty whether the Whigs will be able to maintain their ground in England. But the great cause of all the difficulty is the doubt as to whether we shall go on here, or whether a new revolu" tion must speedily break forth. The cure for all this is evident ; but will the remedy be applied 1 I doubt it much. Nay> I should say, no, it will not. The cure is in a return to the principles of 1830, and to the men and measures, national policy add system of that period. But as that remedy will not be resorted to þÿ the crisis may last a long time. Your obedient servant. O. P. Q.

From the Barbadian , May 31. BONE MANURE. worthy the attention op planters.

Oltcn as we have alluded in tins journal to the latent virtues and growing importance of bone manure, we have a few words to say on the subject still. Years have now elapsed since it was currently said of an application which, however unpromising in appeaiance, is most potent in reality, that it had added 5s. per acre to the value of all the light and sharper soils in the south of Scotland ; but that, we suspect, was too low a calculation ; and wherever the land is of easy access to man and beast, three half-crowns or a trifle more may be safely substituted for the former number. Portability in manures, as in many things else, is a leading virtue ; and wherever the elevation of the land is such as to oppose an insurmountable barrier to the transport and application ot ashes, cow and stable manure, it would be difficult to set limits to the value of an article, the qualities of which were so long hidden that few things in the world were considered more proverbially worthless than " dry hones." But mark the change. Steeps which for centuries grew nothing but grass, and grass too of inferior quality, are now covered in regular rotation with turnips, oats, barley, and even wheat, and, allowing for some difference of climate (the effect of which is felt more or less in backward seasons), are all but undistinjjuishnhle from the plains below. Up till IS28 or the following year, 32 bushels of crushed bones were considered equal to 20 cubical vards of stable dung, and each respectively the requisite ma-

nure for an acre of ground þÿ a difference in portability which may be expressed by 1 to 30, without the slightest exaggeration. If one cubical yard of thoroughly made manure be considered a sufficient load for a horse and cart, twenty such conveyances would be required to transport from town to country the quantity named ; and supposing it fairly deposited on the farm, the grand question is, how many horses will find it hard enough work to convey the load up hill. Thirty we should consider a moderate number, and when to these we add the labour of two scatterers to each cart, the expense of tolls, extra feeding, and other items, the reader will at once perceive the total impossibility of manuring, on the olden principle, mountain land. 1 he expense, in fact, was so enormous, that thing was rarely if ever attempted ; while with bones the case is so different, that the horse and cart and man that bring the article from the mill can take it to the place of its destination ; and when there, go over an acre of land with greater ease than GO persons could do with ordinary dung. Nor is this all ; for although 32 or 34 bushels ol bones pr. acre were very generally usedat first, experience has shown that so large a quantity is not at all necessary, hand is ulwavs gratclul for favours conferred, and never forgets the first benefit ; and hence the discovery, that from 20 to 25 bushels stimulate just as well as the original quantity. Such, in fact, is now the general practice, and it is further

considered a good plan to deposit in drills or furrows common manure first, and then spread a sprinkling of bone on the top. In this way there is action and reaction, and the fermentation natural to one article affects the

other favourably, by bringing its latent virtues sooner into play. In some parts of England two quarters per acre, or 1G bushels, is considered sufficient, and a writer in the Mark Lane Express strongly recommends mixing crushed bones with coal ashes passed through riddle, that the finer parts may he a taken, and the rougher rejected. From all this, it is plain that extreme portability is the leading virtue of hone manure, and there can be no doubt that it is on the streuglh of this quality chiefly that so many upland hills and steeps in almost every county in Scotland, previously bare even of blades, have been reclaimed almost from a state of nature to a state of great and growing fertility þÿ vastly to the augmentation of the agricultural wealth and resources of the country Well, therefore, may we repeat a few of the remarks made in this paper, on the same subject, as far back as July 1828 : þÿ " The time has been when the bones of animals were something like the sticks that prop up peas þÿ useful in serving a temporary purpose, but cumbrous and unsightly, if not a nuisance, ' from the moment the surrounding o fruit was gathered. While the butcher, iu the case of a Highland bullock, contrived to make his own of the beef, the tanner of the hide, and the tinker of the horns, the bones were supposed to have served every purpose after they had passed from the parlour to the hall, and been stripped of every tiling eatable about them. But new lights are constantly streaming on this wonderful world of ours ;

and within the last twenty years, bones of all sorts and sizes, when crushed into a gritish sort of dust, have been found to be an excellent substitute for manure, and, as such, form a regular article of commerce. Fortuhility, in a word, forms the great recommendation of the article in question Like the condensed chemical soups carried out by Captain Barry, it contains much substance in little bulk, and lessens in no mean degree the expense of tolls as well as of labour. To the farmer more particularly, whose grounds are at once so hilly and remote, that dung, unless made at home, can only be procured at a heavy expense, it offers at all times so valuable a substitute, that, in place of scourging his arable land, he may follow the most approved system of husbandry by taking only one white crop at a time. Home, indeed, may fancy that as the demand increases, bones will become so scarce that the dearth of the article will operate as a complete prohibition. But of this we have no fears whatever. Care in collecting and preserving will do much, and the deficit may at all times be supplied from abroad. It was near the end of the fourteenth century before linen rags were manufactured into paper, and as weaving happens to be an old invention, all the cast-linen in Christendom must have previously shared the fate of the weeds of the field, if we except the inconsiderable portion which the descendants ol Galen scraped into caddis. War occasionally made the paper-maker pay

dear for the raw material ; but it was then that he hit upon other expedients, such as using a different article for his coarser fabrics, and husbanding 'the remnants of gentlemen's shirts for those delicious reams of post, whether gilt-edged or plain, upon which lovers breathe their vows, and statesmen indite acts of Parliament." Around Hull, and in other parts of England, bones have been used as manure for a period ol nearly thirty years; and it is a curious

fact, that while the Scots have the reputation of being the best farmers in the world, almost all our great improvements are imported from the sister country. From Hull, the practice travelled to East Lothian, and was for years so stationary that not a single bushel of the new manure was seen in the south of Scotland till 1825. þÿ Dumfries and Galloway Courier.

My son þÿ I shall he gone, and you will have the management of the concern þÿ Never expect to sustain your paper upon any other foundation than its merit- Be prudent, temperate and upright Work hard. After the failure of the manccuvre ol throwing his army between that of Schwartzenberg and Germany, in the vain hope of inducing that general to make a retrograde movement, and so gain time for the better fortification of Paris, and enable him to avail himself of the numerous reinforcements which were marching to his assistance, Napoleon, attended by a few stall' officers and a considerable body of cavalry, approached Paris by the Fontainbleau road, lie left the army with the view of trying the effect of negotiation, as a last resource, to endevour, by the enthusiasm which he thought his presence would inspire in his capital, by a determined resistence to make the best terms he could. When he arrived at Cour de France, a pretty hamlet about 12 miles from Paris, he found the country overrun by detachments of Cossacks, who seemed very industrious jn paying ofl old scores. Fearing his personal liberty, if not safety might be endangered by advancing further, he alighted at a miserable auberge, and there waited with apparent confidence for the answer of Alexander to the terms of accomodation he had offered. In a corner of the apartment, in which the emperor and his officers were assembled, lay the only remaining son of the hostess in the agonies of death. Napoleon was by the bed side at the moment the poor lad breathed his last, and when it was ascertained that he was no more, he turned evidently in a state of terrible agitation, to General De la Chasse and exclaimed or

rather shrieked " Cest fini pour nous deux," "We are both done for." He had scarcely repeated the words when a courier arrived with the news that the combined armies of Europe had entered Paris, and that he had ceased to reign. The death bed scene seemed to have prepared him for this announcement, for seeing the poor woman of the house in a state of distraction from excessive grief, he kindly took her by the hand and endea. voured to console her in the most collected and humane manner, but she would not be comforted; and in leaving he was heard to exclaim, " Poor woman your loss is greater than mine, for it is irretrievable." He mounted his horse and returned to Fontainbleau, first having desired one of his aids-de-camp to give her 500f. Two years ago this anecdote was related to us by the object of the Emperors compassion and bounty, who although she had lost two sons in his wars, seemed still to entertain a warm feeling of gratitude for such extraordinary kindness.

THE BEAUTIFUL INCOGNITO. What beautiful forms occasionally pass us in the streets, faces that haunt our thoughts for days, but are never seen again, shooting by us their brightness sudden as a fallen star, Sve just catch a glance of its trailing light þÿ a long waving ringlet, and its dart into some doorway ushered in by hard knocks, or vanishes into the dark portals of a carriage. þÿ What conjectures we sometimes form as we walk behind a graceful woman, who moves on in all the majesty of a J uno, or sweeps the pavement like a Nyrnph gliding along with noiseless footsteps, as if pacing the clouds. þÿ Then to see one, apparently lost in the streets, yet too modest to enquire her way, shunning the gaze of passengers with averted head, yet seeming anxious to find some honest face to which she dare risk enquiry. Such a one I passed the other day in Oxford street, there was something foreign in her features, her beautiful face was tinged with the sunny hues of Italy ; it brought up images of the land, " of the rose and the myrtle," of gondolas and guitars such forms as Praxiteles has rendered immortal ; her ringlets reminded you of the vineyard, oftendrils waving in the rich breath of Zephyr, there was music and song in her motion. Her eyes too " were dark with excessive bright," and her long hair fell in luxuriant curls down her graceful neck ; there was also a peculiar lightness in her step, an elasticity like the springing of a wild deer, conjuring up dances that you have dreamed of in marble halls among perfumed lamps and

open lettices. " The mind, the music breathing from her face, And oh! that eye was in itself a soul I" But there was something apparently abstracted in her look ; for a moment her eyes swept the long range of carriages, as though she had missed her own. Several young gallants also dared to upraise sundry glasses to their eyes, like astronomers, who had discovered some new wonder in the heavens, but she frowned not at their insolence No ; her face would have stood the scrutiny of Kings and Princes and only smiled, as she did then, upon their insulting curiosity. For a moment she stood near the edge of the pavement, and looked down Regent street, but no carriage appeared to take her up ; still she was not oflended, but placed a white-kid-covered finger on her thin lips. She seemed like Patience on a monument smiling to herself, or like Ellen Tree in the Jewess, just wakening to a consciousness of Ruben's absence. At length she walked down the street with a rapid step, until all on a sudden her ears were arrested by the sound of a guitar, and a young Italian singing ; how her eves brightened at the sight, perchance that sound reminded her of her lovely home by the lake of Como ; she seemed entranced, and but for the beating of time to the muse by her small feet, you might have taken her for a statute. " With head raised, and look up intent, And eye and ear attentive bent, And looks flung back, and lips apart, Like monument of Grecian art."4 She soon attracted more attention than the

musician, and one youth so far forget himself as to point to her foot ; but she gave the poor singer something wrapt up in paper. It could not be less than a crown, no þÿ a penny forsooth 1 fingers like her s were formed aloric to touch gold and þÿsilver not vile copper,

bastsjr Tas'jasroasjR ma®aama»«a atss. which but for a moment before I he street sweeper might have converted into a bun at the confectioner's which she had entered. True, there might be something not quite in unison with the bon ton, in her beating time to the music, but then 1 thought of the beloved Italy, how beauty and enthusiasm are blended in the bosoms of those born under sunny skies, and these thoughts increased my interest for the lovely stranger, although others had smiled at this negligence. She moved along in all her natural gracefulness, occasionally exchanging a smile with moustaehiod nonpereils, but these of course were Earls or Marquesses, whom she had met at Almack's, or the opera, or the Levee. For one so nobly formed would not deign to arch the ivory of her neck to anything beneath these. I followed her footsteps, determined that if any insult was offered to one so lovely, I would resent it. For she might be a princess, a foreigner, and while dreaming of her native land, had forgotten the precise spot where she left her carriage, for she still continued to glance upon those that thundered past. At length her sandal became unloosed and proved an impediment to her walking and looked round but no footman appeared ; her pace became slower ; she kept nearer to the shop windows, but never offered to enter ; and the long satin riband, " like a younded ! snake, drew its slow length along." I felt in torture, for many an eye was drawn downward to view her disaster, but not one gallant enough to kneel and remove it. She paused

by the corner of a palisade. She look at her foot, then around: there were but few passing ; and, like Raleigh of old, when he threw down his rich cloak at the feet of his maiden Queen, I so 1 rushed forward, and planting one knee upon the pavement, with all the grace 1 possessed, I looked into her face and said " allow ! me fair lady " She made no answer, but smi led, and extended her fairy foot, and I soon twined the envious string around her small ! ankle. Another smile, and she was gone, I still remained kneeling, and caught another glance at her feet in the distance. I could have sworn to them among a thousand. She had exchanged a nod with a red fared old gentleman, who hud witnessed my gallantry, and looked on me as I knelt, with a very peculiar expression. I rose and watche'd his glance narrowly ; it came from the corner of his eye, there was a mixture of roguish knowingness in it, a kind of secret triumph 1 and just as he passed me with averted head, 1 and the same queer look, his eye caught a j glance at certain particles of dirt imprinted on my knee ; and the ruddy old wretch gave a loud ah ! ah 1 ah ! ah ! which was re-cchoed by a host of " jarves" from the coach-stand. But England is proverbial for its rudeness : bad I done such a thing in the gardens of Paris, 1 should have been rewarded with glances from an hundred bright eyes. I minded not their laughter ; I bore the badge of servitude upon my knee as proudly as Sir Walter bore the print of the queenly footsep

upon his cloak. 1 would not have rubbed it oft for a kingdom. Then her eyes, the associations of Italy, her dignity, the missing of her liveried servants, the emblazonry of her carriage, her enthusiasm at sight of the poor minstrel with his guitar. I walked along in the halo of a sonnet, illuminated by her beauty, for I bad knelt at her feet, where princes might feel honored in being allowed to prostrate themselves. I walked along, she again passed mc ; 1 felt ashamed, the colour mounted

my forehead, she turned as if to speak ; thetts was a divinity in her countenance, 1 held down my head, I dearcd not have looked on her. She passed, 1 felt dizzy ; perhaps she iritented to acquaint nie with the loss of her carriage ; wished me to escort her home ; to take her arm ; to walk by her side, to h< nr her speak. Regent street seemed to reel I came in contact with a porter, his burthen hit my head; it awoke me to a consciousness of my situation. 1 ventured to look after her, she was several yards from me. I saw her feet, they had resumed their former elasticity, no sandal was unbound ; oh that she had dropped a pin, her glove, her bonnet, anything to have left me another chance to have accosted her. Alas, she went on, she turned, look at me again. Generous Italian ! enthusiastic Princess ! I had done her a slight service ; she had come from a sunny land, not from the frigid north ; she could not forget it. She wa3 " a beauty and a mystery," and I followed her without knowing why. Poetry or romance, or madness, had spell-bound me. She seemed alone though in London. At length the sky grew black, and a few big drops fell upon the pavement, 1 watdhed narrowlv ; she put up her beautiful parasol, its rich greenness added to her loveliness ; she seemed like a rose under an arbour of woodbine. She paused, lifted her sublime eyes to the sky. The rain increased, she looked in vain for her carriage. She now stood at the corner of a street, a hackney coachman caught her eye, and alighted from

his box. I was not near enough to hear their conversation, and they entered þÿ There are places called " gin palaces" þÿ temples dedicated to juniper þÿ this was one of them ! The villain had doubtless informed her that it was some hotel, and persuaded her to wait there until he got his coach in readiness, and she, a beautiful foreigner, knew but little of English manners, perhaps could not speak the language perfectly, she might be imposed upon, be driven to a wrong place. No, I would not allow it, and entered the gin-shop just in time to þÿ The beautiful Incognito was raising to her lips þÿ just lifting þÿ to those lips þÿ No, if I were to be put to the torture, I could not write another syllable. þÿ T. Miller.

Getting into Debt. þÿ There is no error into which the young and thoughtless so easily fall, as that of creating debts The facility with which this is at first accomplished, seems to have blinded them as to the consequences. They fondly imagine that it will be always as easy to escape from, as to incur them. Not so Dr. Franklin truly remarked that the debtor is the slave of iho creditor, since the former is bound by the laws of God and man to fulfil every such obligation He, who therefore places himself in this position knows what he has to expect at the day of payment, and he has no right, to complain of any consequence he has rashly brought upon himself. Better, far better, to live on bread and water, and he independent, than incur any debt w ithout the means of payment. One half the ills of life arises from the thoughtlessness of debtors, and the demands, of their deservedly incensed creditors. But let not those rail at their fellow men as the cause of j their misfortunes, who bring them so heedlessly upon themselves.

MAY 31, 1837. THE RIGHT HON. LORD BEXLEY IN THE CHAIR. Rev. Dr. PHILIP, from South Africa. þÿ My Lord, Ladies, and Gentlemen, 1 remember having read, in an old book, an account of a Persian monarch who was receiving gifts from his subjects, on a royal progress through his kingdom ; and a poor man, who had nothing else to give, ran to a brook, filled his hand with water, brought the water to his sovereign, and begged him to accept of it, ns the expression of his heart. I know not, My Lord, whether I shall have as much to present to this Society as that poor subject gave to his king: but I am happy to have this opportuni ty expressing my own gratitude to the So- of ciety for the Bibles sent to Africa; for the generous supply we have had of the word of God ; for the benefit which our Missionary Labourers and Institutions have derived from the assistance afforded us hy the Society ; and to present to vour Lordship, and this Society, the gratitude of the Hottentots, and Slaves, and Apprentices, who have received vour Bibles, read your Bibles, and render you thanks for them. And, My Lord, warmer thanks have never been presented on the altar of this Society, than those which are rising to God, every day, from the hearts of those people, for the books they have received. When the Rev. Mr Frazer was addressing you, I recollected a happy thought of Mr Wilbcrforcc, who represented Africa ns pleading in chains, before the House of Commons, for her rights. \ou have had this dav a scene that would have delighted the heart of that distinguished philanthropist ; yea. that

now delights his heart in þÿheaven for we have no reason to suppose that he is unacquainted with what is passing here on the present occasion. You have seen Africa, pleading for freedom, not in chains, but with chains broken, and free ; not only free in point law, of but having the slave-chain of sin broken also þÿ a free man giving vou here, in person, his grateful acknowledgments for what England has done, and what this Society has done, both for his soul and for his body. When men are in want, they know the value of bread ; and none can know the value of the Scriptures like those who have suffered a famine of the word of God. One of the peculiar features of the Slaves and Hottentots and Apprentices in South Africa is, their high value for the word of God þÿ the delight with which they speak of the word of God. They esteem the word of God as invaluable ; and I have never heard any class of persons speak with such feeling, and so much gratitude, for the word of God, as these people. 1 may perhaps mention here, as I must hereafter, our wants. We have, at this time, several Stations still destitute of the word of God: and while we thank you, My Lord, and this Society, for the liberal manner in which we have been entrusted with Bibles, and the liberal donations granted us, I must add, that we have great demands to make. Hitherto slaves have been obtainable when free labour has not. The attempt to raise such commodities as sugar, cotton, & rice within the tropics, by means of free labour, coloured labour I mean has never yet made. It is very well to assume that none but slaves have hither done so : but it appears to me, that if the blacks, to whom the climate is suitable were prevented from obtaining land, whether in the United States or in our own West Indies, they would work like a workmen here for wages ; they would work in combination ; and the very circumstance of their being free would induce the capitalists, instead of trusting all to the sweat of the labouricr, to trust more to bis own invention, to improvements of cultivation and I speak only of that the cultivation of sugar may proceed in the West Indies us done, and perhaps better. A very general alarm was felt throughout this Island on Sunday night last from the tempestuous state of the weather From an early hour of the morning, the wind blew fresh from the North East þÿ we should rather think it was almost due North, It increased every succeeding hour of the day, became exceedingly boisterous in the afternoon, and by eight o'clock, came in such tremendous gusts as to give fearful indications of an approaching hurricane. The violence of the wmd increased to a most alarming degree by ten o'clock, when it moderated, and we had an hour of comparative quietness, with drizzling rain We expected, however, that a change of wind was approaching, and so ii proved ; for at eleven it rose again from an opposite quarter, the South, and blew with terrific violence until about three in the mor. ning, accompanied by heavy rain, with several vivid flashes o< lightning and distant thunder. Sunday night was an awful one ; few persons, we believe, retired to their beds until the violence of the gale had subsided1 That the daylight arrived with a serene þÿsky and a fresh, but no alarming breeze from the South, and that our houses were uninjured, was a mercy of Providence for which we ought to be most thankful. The only injuiy in town has been that of two vessels driven on shore on the reef to leeward of the town, þÿ the Myrtle and the Ruth, both of w hich, we hear, are total wrecks. Had the gale blown with similar violence from the S. W., the

loss of shipping would, probably, have been very severe. Much injury, however, we regret to hear, has been sustained on Estates in the country. It is saidþÿ we can only state matters by common report, for our Country frienas have furnished very little information, þÿ that the following properties have sufferedþÿ Bloomsbury Estate þÿ the upper works of the mill blown over þÿ Still-house down, and half the Boiling- house. Mill Tops thrown down on Carringtons , Exchange, Mellowes, Saltram, Clnmborazxo, Sea View, Easy Hall, Mr. þÿDonovan s, Highland, Parks, and Mallards, Bawdens and the Hirer, the property of Sir R A. Alleyne, in St. Andrew's þÿ Ridgeway and the Farm, Points injured Windsor, one Point in- þÿ jured. þÿ Many others have had their Chimneys thrown down, and other injury to Boiling-houses, and many negro houses thrown down, or stripped of their covering þÿ plantain trees down, and the Indian corn much injured þÿ At the Society » Cow-house thrown down, and one cow killed, and another much injured. The building used as a place of worship in St. Joseph's, blown down. We shall have, probably, tardier accounts of damage done in the country. The hurricane seasons may truly be said to have commenced, but at a remarkably early period. To those, in whose minds the horrors of the 11th August, 1831 must be still vivid, the appearance of last Sunday naturally produced awe and tear; but many of us were so wonderfully preserved on that fatal morning, when our houses fell at our

very feet, that there w-as great room for Hope still in the mercy of Goo in the midst of judgement. The change of weather in the inqrning of Monday last was indeed an unspeakable relict. We hope that we shall not receive bad accounts from the Islands to the Northward. We must however, feel some anxiety about their..

Barbados Mercury, July 15. It is with great regret we have learned, since our last, by well authenticated accounts from the country, that the injury done to the mills and buildings of some estates, by the high wind of Sunday, is more extensive and serious than we thought there was any reason to apprehend, from what we experienced of it, in town. The truth however is, that where such damage has been done, the mills were with their points up, the crop of sugar on the estate not being finished, and the wind having therefore much greater power upon the upper works, they have, as it were, gone off' by the run. Much inconvenience, we understand, is likely toarise to the suffering estates, in consequence of their being now without the means of getting through w ith the balance of their crops þÿ some having as much as twenty hogsheads of sugar still to make unless þÿ assisted by some kind neighbour more fortunate than themselves. Much indeed have the inhabitants of the island, generally, to be thankful for, to a kind Providence, who, remembering mercy in the midst of judgment, stayed the storm that was ready to burst upon us, and saved us from that distress which would inevitably have been the result of a visitation similar in its violence to that of August, 1831, when the bosom of destruction swept over our then flourishing island, and involved us all in ruin and dismay. Had the wind, it is imagined by some old experienced folks in such matters, shitted its point from east of Dorth to north west, or gone to the opposite point of south

west, the whole island would have been laid waste, and for the third time since 1831, such a dispensation would have brought with it all the horrors and the privations experienced as the consequence a of the two former, or at any rate the calamitous effects of the August hurricane þÿ a scene of suffering, which all who witnessed that awful night must well remember. The two schooners, the Myrtle and Ruth, noticed in our last as having driven on shore on the night of Sunday, have since become complete wrecks ; they have both been sold at public auction, the former on Wednesday and the latter on the day following. WILLIAMS. þÿ I did not anticipate, My Lord, the pleasure ol' again addressing this Meeting on behalf of the British and Foreign Bible Society ; but it affords me very great gratification to see your Lordship heie, and so many noble Lords, and Dignitaries, and other Gentlemen convened ; and I do anticipate the period, when every Nobleman in our land will esteem it an honour and a privilege to be identified with the labours which the British and Foreign Bible Society contemplates. At that Meeting, bis Lordship had described his visit to the South-Sea

Islands: stating, that, in passing from the Sandwich-Islands' group to South America, he had happened to light on an Island which he imagined was not before discovered : the boats were lowered, and the officers had specific orders to be cautious in their intercourse with the people, as, in all probability, they were savages. But soon after, a canoe appeared, with two goodlooking natives in it. They came on board the ship; and presented a document from a Missionary, stating that they were Native Teachers, employed to impart the knowledge Salvation to the inhabi- of tants of that Island. His Lordship went on shore : and was conducted through a wood. When he had proceeded about two miles, a wide lawn opened out before him ; and in the centre of this lawn stood a spacious Chapel, and some native cottages, appearing to peep at him through the luxuriant foliage of the bread fiuit banana trees in which they were embowered. His Lordship was then conducted into a cottage, which lie described as very clean and respectable: and on a table in one of these cottages, the habitation of the Native Missionary, his Lordship recognised a portion of the New Testament in the native language. His Lordship had given a most interesting account, which was reported by the Clergyman last year: and when he sat clown, I had the happiness of standing up, and introducing myself to the Meeting as the individual who -discovered the Island, introduced Christianity to the inhabitants, and trans-

I would say one or two words more. þÿ I anticipate, that by this time next year, I shall he on the other side of the globe. From the Barbadian, July 27, 1837. bridge- town, thursday july 27. Tiie events which have occurred from Tuesday the 25th to the afternoon of yesterday invest our paper of this day with a threefold interest. With an awful sense of the power of the Almighty God, in whom all his Creatures "live, and move, and have their being," " and without whom, not a sparrow falls to the ground" and fervent gratitude for the unspeakable mercies of that God, we proceed to narrate the extraordinary events of the two last days. The whole island has been already informed of the arrival of the Ringdove Brig of war, with despatches to our Governor communicating the melancholy intelligence of the death of our venerable King on the 20th of June, and of the accession of her Majesty, Queen Alexandria Victoria, a niece of King William, and daughter of the late Duke of Kent, to the Throne. The nation has lost a Sovereign who was universally beloved for the many amiable qualities of the heart, and for his anxious desire, though little was left in his own power to do, for the promotion of the best interests of his people. It is impossible to foresee the political consequences of this event ; an event, however, which the advanced age of the King gave reason to expect. T he people of .England seem to indulge in the most favourable anticipations of their happiness under the reign of their youthful Queen, whose education is said to be of such a character as eminently to qualify her for a just performance of her high duties, and whose mind is said to be formed

in a religious and virtuous mould. What in fluence the Uight Honorable Noblemen and Gentlemen, forming the administration of the Country, may have on the feelings of Her Majesty, it is as yet impossible to judge. We hope, that our Sovereign Lady, young as she :s, is blessed with discernment and penetration to see into the tortuous and dangerous policy ol those who at present guide the helm of affairs, and will, by an early and decided exercise of her authority, revive the hopes of that great portion of her people whose desire is, to preserve, unimpaired and uncontaminated, the sacred and time-honoured union between the Church and the State, and to protect the Church of England from the desperate attacks of her enemies. O may this accomplished scion of an illustrious race inherit the uncompromising integrity, the unbending firmness, and the single minded heart of her grandfather, the great and good George the Third, who, firm as a rock, could never be moved by political sophistry, by specious liberalism, by the rude assaults of the Republican, or the profane wit of the Infidel, from the straight path of duty. The melancholy intelligence of the King's decease was announced on Sunday last by the firing of minute guns from the Ringdove as she came into Carlisle Bay. It was a remarkable circumstance, that, at thp very moment when the Minister in the desk at St. Mary's read tire prayer in the Litany for the spiritual and temperal welfare of King William, the first minute gun proclaimed his de-

parture from this world. Seventy one guns were fired, corresponding to the number of years our Sovereign had lived. The colours on all the signal stations, and the flags of all the vessels, were hall-masted immediately on the announcement of the event ; and when all due compliment had been paid to the de-

The particulars of the King's death, the pro clamation of the Queen, &c &c., as they appear in the Globe of Monday (for we were not so fortunate as to obtain any paper by the Ringdove). We have inserted in our present sheet. On Monday his Excellency the Commander-in-Chief, having held a Privy Council on Sunday evening, issued his command for the appearance ot the Corps of Life Guards, and the Royal Regt. of Militia Foot Guards at the King's House on Tuesday, to attend the public proclaiming of her Majesty Queen Victoria. The Life Guards mustered at 10 o'clock in Trafalgar Square, and the Foot Guards in Beckvvith Square, & between 11 & 12 proceeded, þÿ the former to Government House to escort his Excellency and the latter to the ground at King's House, Captain Phillips, cemmanding the Royal Regiment, drew the battalion upon the South side of the ground, and a guard of honour of the 30th Regiment from the Garrison, was drawn up opposite to the Royal Regiment of Militia þÿ About one o'clock his Excellency Sir E. J. M. M'Gregor. in the full dress of the Windsor Uniform, escorted by the Life Guards, and attended by his suite, the Colonial Aides de amp, and the Colonial Statf, arrived, and was met by Sir Samford Whittingham, Coinmander-of the Forces, and his suite, with the heads of the military departments. The

Lord Bishop and the Clergy, with the public officers of the island, and many private gentlemen, were on the steps of the King's House to receive his Excellency, who very soon after his arrival proceeded to a spot between the positions of the King's troops and the militia, accompanied by the Lord Bishop and Clergy, and other of the numerous body of gentlemen assembled on the occasion, when Her Majesty was duly proclaimed by the Serjeant-at arms, Benjamin Walrond, Esq. The Band of the 36th Regiment then struck up God save the King," the multitude gave " three huzzas, the Militia Artillery, stationed on the Eastern side of the avenue to King's House, fired 21 guns, and the Royal Regiment a Feu de Joie. His Excellency the Governor then dismounted, held a Levee at King's House, and soon after returned to Government House, escorted by the Life Guards, under a complement of 21 guns from the Artillery. We must here remark how well the Artillery pieces were served on this occasion under the command of the veteran Captain Francis The Proclamation of the Queen's accession was afterwards circulated by beat of drum thiough the town.

Short-sighted mortals as we all are, who could have expected that such a scene as the above would be tbliowed in a few hours by the afflicting occurrences which we are now to relate. About half-past eleven o'clock of Tuesday night, the cry of " Fire" in the streets, and the dismal tones of the Fire Bell, roused every family in town, and many out of town, from their beds When we came out to the front of our house, looking to the South and East the illumination of the sky, and the reflection from the flames on the tops of the houses and trees was awfully splendid. It was evident, though the alarm hud been given so short a

time ago, that a fire had been raging to a considerable extent sonic where in the Bay-street. We proceeded as fast as possible to the direction in which the fire appeared to be, and found that several houses in the Bay between the Police Station and Mr. Lee's residence, Sand House, were in flames. An immense crowd had assembled, but, except from the active exertions of the immediate neighbours, nothing was done to arrest the fearful progress of the fire. Two of the Town Engines arrived, þÿ we suppose as soon as it w as possible to get them drawn, þÿ and the Police were in attendance, who doubtless made every possible exertion, while surrounded by such a dense mob, to save the adjoining þÿproperty.- Soon after, most fortunately, a strong force from the Garrison came down with an Engine. The order and discipline of a regular force always effects what numbers, without concert, without discipline, without system, alarmed, terrified, and bewildered, can never accomplish. The Town Engines were worked with all zeal and good intention, no doubt ; but we understand that the Garrison Engine, with the extraordinary exertions of the Engineers, and seamen, rendered the most important service. These men rushed into the very flames, for the purpose of pulling down adjoining houses ; and it is reported, þÿ but we cannot vouch for the fact, and hope it is not correct, þÿ that one man was so burned by the fire as to cause his death. The Lord Bishop was present, and repeatedly cheered the

people on, who were striving to extinguish the fire. The fire, we are informed, commenced in an ironing room of the house occupied by Captain Howell, formerly of the mail boat service. It is very extraordinary that the flames should have got to a most alarming height before Mr. II or his family were aware ol it. We hear that a coal-pot was left in the room with burning coals, supposed to ha\e been not carefully extinguished, but how- the fire was communicated no one in the house can tell. We are told that Mr. Howell, when he went into the room, found the roof in flames, but no fire any where under the roof. We reeret to say that his house was entirely consumed, with Mrs. Faulkner's, Mr. \\ mite s (Blacksmith) and Mr. Benskin's. þÿ For all these individuals we feel deeply - þÿ- Mrs. Faulkner is a widow, who has several limes experienced severe affliction and loss, and is a deserving industrious woman, with children, whom she has at great pains and expense bad educated. Mr Benskin has before been unfoitunate in losing a valuable vessel in the hurricane of 1831. Mr. White is an industrious man of family. Sand House was in imminent danger. Though in some measure protected by the trees and shrubbery, and being farther in from the road, yet if the adjoining buildings had not been taken down, it would probably have caught fire. We should thank God that there was little wind, and that North East, which blew in a direction towards the sea. A South wind would have been fatal to the whole of (he lower
part of the Bay, and the houses leading to the Pier. Notwithstanding the extraordinary exertions made to extinguish the lire, it was not finally extinct until yesterday forenoon.

A most melancholy duly now devolves upon us, that ol relating another severe nale of wind, the second in the short space of 17 days, which has caused a dreadful destruction of property. Before the fire which v\o iiave

described above was entirely subdued, a north or N. E wind began towards the morning of yesterday to blow with a violence which at this season of the year is always alarming. It soon, however, shifted to the South East, and then to South and blew with tremendous fury. Another hurricane, and its consequent calamities, seemed every hour approaching. The aale came on at about the same hour, and from nearly the same points of the compass, as that of the 3d September 1835. By the mercy of God, however, a considerably abatement of the wind took place after the hour of noon. On land little damage has been done, the injuries being chiefly confined to the throwing down of palings in town, the breaking off boughs of trees, <&c. and in the Country, we understand, many negro houses are blown down, some chimneys of boiling houses, and the Indian Corn, and some Canes prostrate ; but we trust not materially injured. The destruction ot shipping, however, is truly deplorable. We here subjoin the melancholy list of Vessels stranded, which has been kindly supplied to us by a gentl :man whose information can be strictly depended upon : þÿ vessei.s stranded, 26th july, 1837. S. ; French schooner Jean Camille, , Guadeloupe ; Sir Henry Warde, Miller, Berbiee ; sloops Amelia, Cox, Saint Lucia ; Eleanor, Dodd, Antigua ; Messenger, M'Carty, 1 rinidad ; mail-boat Tickler , M'Alpin, ; sloop Fortitude, Best, Tobago : 11. M. Steamer Alban, Lieut. Tinling, . vessels in the bay, which bode it out and put to sea. II M. Ship Gannett, Whish commander þÿ rode it out; 11. M. Packet Spry, Lieutenant James þÿ rode it out; ship Britannia, Simmons Bristol þÿ rode it out, but strained, and in a very leaky state ; ship Fortitude, Fowle, London þÿ rode it out ; steam vessel City oj Kingston, Barton, Jamaica þÿ rode it out, alterwards put to sea, and returned safe; schooner Elizabeth <$ Esther, Strange, Saint Vincent, rode it out ; ditto Stranger, Piper, Dominica þÿ put to sea, and not returned ; sloop Dove, Thurston, Trinidad rode it þÿ out in Quarantine ; French barque Quatre Freres, Hainneville, Cherbourg put to sea, and not return- þÿ ed. We fear that we shall have to add the Ship Britannia, Capt. Simmons, to the list of vessels lost, as she has started two planks, and is making water, we understand, so fast, that it is a question whether it will be possible to get out the Cargo of Sugar, before she sinks at her moorings. The loss of shipping, and of produce on board, as well as other property, is considerably greater than that mentioned in the hur-

ricane of 11th August 1831. At that time sixteen vessels were lost ; now no less than twenty two are stranded. Language is powerless to describe the extraordinary personal efforts made by gentlemen of the town, and by several negro men, to save the lives of the seamen on board the stranded vessels. þÿ

vatstrnTuutstR. ma©3tama»©3 ATJS. m The scene was a most interesting and affecting one yesterday. His Excellency the Governor rode to the reef where most of the vessels were on shore, rode into the water, and most humanely exerted himself to have ropes conveyed to the seamen on board to save their lives. Amongst the persons engaged in this humane undertaking stood prominent the Editor of the Globe Mr. Dki.nan ; who trusting to his power of body, and expertness in swimming, stemmed the raging waves, and with a humanity and courage which most highly exact him in the opinion of the public, saved several seamen from drowning. We understand that several of the crew of an American brig may have been saved, but they were so stupified, paralyz- so ed by their awful situation that they could not be persuaded to throw out a rope to them who were ready to save their lives þÿ they, poor fellows, met their death. We are informed too, that one of the men saved from drowning was so bruised and wounded by the floating timbers of the wrecks, that he died soon after being brought on shore. þÿ Captain Scott of the Barque Elizabeth was saved in the same manner as his men, but he would not leave the ship till all his crew had got safely to shore. The Militia were called out to protect property, and a detachment of the regular troops came down. The Police are also in attendance to-day with the Koyal Begt. of Militia. These have been sadly harrassed since Tuesday ; the duty of Tuesday at the hottest hours of the day, out again in the

night at the Fire, and on duty yesterday and to day, must be truly fatiguing but we are sure they render these services cheerfully. There is now no calculating upon the season of the year. July is now a hurricane month. We remember a blow on the 22nd July, 1813. when about 10 vessels were driven ashore in Carlisle Bay, the wind being South West. We have had no July gale since, until this year when we have been alarmed by two dreadful ones in the short space of 17 days- How have human expectations and hopes been blighted ! þÿ Many, on the point of embarkation for England, see the beautiful vessels in which they expected to cross the sea safely in a few hours, wrecked on the shore 1 Several vessels amongst them, the Pitscottie, from London, with dry goods, just arrived in safety, from their respective ports, dashed to pieces before their cargoes could be landed ! How soon all the efforts of man, and all his promising schemes of pleasure or of profit may be blasted by the breath of the Almighty. What a lesson should these things teach us of humility, and self abasement; and what a warning is it to us all to be ready for any change which our Heavenly Father may in his wisdom see fit to order for us and ours 1 Every day shews the instability, and precarious tenure of all earthly things : but such awful dispensations as storms and fire ought especially to fix indelibly on our minds the necessity of preparation.

From the Nevis Post, August 2. We deeply sympathize with our friends> for the losses they may this day have have sustained by the tempestuous weather, and we rejoice with them that the threatening appearance assumed by the weather, was not more productive of those calamitous effects, so common at this season ot the year> and so often fatally realized in this part of the world. This morning between the hours of three and four, the wind being to the North, a sho\ver of rain of short duration fell, and at day light was succeeded by another, with a brisk brecse of wind : at I past six the wind began to rise, and was accompanied with rain at repeated intervals, until 8 o'clock. The wind then shifted N. N. W. and gradually increased in gusts until 10 o'clock ; during which time very much rain fell, it then veered to the Westward and to due South, then back to S. W. and lastly back to South, from whence it blew steadily, but with violence to 2 o'clock ; since when it has abated. The vessels in the road that were in a condition for sea got out. The British American Schooner Lady Smith, and Sloop Aid of this port, have been driven on shore, and we learn that the Sloop Esther Maria, also of this port lias been totally wrecked at Indian Castle. We have not heard whether any damage has been done in the Country. In town we are happy to state, that with the exception of a few fences being thrown down, and a few trees that have been uprooted, all things else have escaped injury. þÿ þÿ-»ooo»

On Tuesday morning, the 20th of June instant, at twelve minutes past two o'clock, our late Most Gracious Majesty Sovereign Kin" William the Fourth expired at his Castle of Windsor, in the seventy-second year of his age, and the seventh year of his reign This event has caused one universal feeling of regret and sorrow to his late Majesty's faithful and attached subjects, to whom he was endeared by the deep interest in their welfare which he invariably manifested, as well as bv the many manly virtues which marked and adorned his character. Upon the intimation of this distressing event, the Lords of the Privy Council assembled this day at Kensington-palace, and gave orders for proclaiming her present Majesty, who made a most gracious declaration to them, and caused all the Lords and others of the King's Privy Council who were then present to be sworn of her Majesty's cil. At the Court at Kensington, the 20th day of June, 1837: þÿ Present, the Queen's Most Excellent Majesty in Couucil. Her Majesty being this dav present in Council, was pleased to make the following Declaration, viz: þÿ " The severe and afflicting loss which the nation has sustained by the death of his Majesty, my beloved uncle, has devolved upon ine the duty of administering the government ot this empire This awful responsibility is imposed upon me so suddenly, and at so early a period of my lile, that I should feel myself utterly oppressed by the burden were I not sustained by the "hope that Divine Providence, which has called me to this work, will give me strength for the performance of it, and that 1 shall find in the purity of my iutentions, and in my zeal for the public welfare, that support and those resources which usually belong to a more mature age, and to longer experience. " 1 place my firm reliance upon the wisdom of Parliament, and upon the loyalty and affection ol my people. 1 esteem it also a peculiar advantage that I succeed to a Sovereign whose constant regard for the rights and liberties of his subjects, and whose desire to promote the amelioration of the laws and institutions of the country, have rendered his name the object of general attachment and veneration. "Educated in England, under the tender and enlightened care of a most attached mother, I have learned from mv infancy to respect and love the constitution of mv native country. " It will be my unceasing study to maintain

the reformed religion as by the law established, securing at the same time to all the full enjoyment of religious liberty, and 1 shall steadily protect the rights, and promote to the utmost of my power the happiness and welfare, of all classes of my subjects." Whereupon the Lords of the Council made it their humble request to her Majesty, that her Majesty's most gracious Declaration to their Lordships might he made public, which her Majesty was pfoased to order accordingly. "Windsor, Tuesday Evening þÿ No idea can be formed of the state of gloom into which the town is thrown by the death of his Majesty. Very soon after the melancholy event took place the whole ol the establishment ol the Castle were introduced to the room where the remains of his Majesty were, for the purpose ol allowing them uu opportunity to take a last look at their Royal Master. Many of the old domestics were very much affected, and almost all of them shed tears. Sonic complaints have been made owing to the so crecy that was observed relative to the condition of his Majesty : hut it appears that this is n fresh proof of his Majesty's kind and benevolent disposition. Being aware of the effect which the statement of the real aspect of his malady would have upon trade, and the suspension ol business it would occasion,

l S3 he was certainly anxious that no allusion should he made to it, and it was only when the necessity for it became very urgent that he consented to the publication of bulletins. Shortly after his Majesty had breathed his last remains were removed from the apartment he had rccenly occupied to a room in the next wing of the Castle, where some few persons were admitted to see them, and to take a last view of their Sovereign. His Majesty was lying upon a small French bedstead, enveloped in a white covering, The -head was bandaged round, and nothing hut the countenance was until after the funeral " visible.
