The waves rolled mountain high in Carlisle Bay, lashing the roek bound pier and adjacent shores in awful grandeur, and sending their spray full a hundred feet high. Out of twenty eight vessels, large and small, which were riding safely at their anchorage at seven o'clock, twenty two were driven on shoref and most of them dashed on the ledge of rocks reaching from below the stores of Messrs. Moore to the upper reef lying in some places in heaps of four or five, large and small, from the humble sloop to the 'ofty and capacious barque or brig, exposed, many of them, with their sides down, or keels upwards, to the violence of the surf, which dashed for the greater part of the day, with unabated fury, against themt driving the large upon the smaller vessels, and thus completing the work of destruction to its utmost finish. Some again were driven by the force of the wind and violence of the sea, upon the rocks abreast of the Pier, and there have become complete wrecks Along the shore for above a mile and a half may be seen the remnants of the shattered vessels and their cargoes pilled up in heaps, and indeed wherever the eye turns, one unvaried scene of ruin and devastation is presented. Never we believe, in the memory of the oldest inhabitant of the island, has a shipwreck occurred in so short a time, so calamitous in its consequences. Only one vessel was able, during the height of the gale, to succeed in clearing the bay ; this was the City of Kingston, steamer, which had arrived

here a few days previous. Her commander, it is generally observed, displayed excellent seamanship upon the occasion, and considering all circumstances, that the wind was blowing into the harbour direct, and the sea running so high that the wheels required an additional impetus to keep her in progress the effort was one of great hazard, and the success which fortunately crowned it, entitles him to great credit. His Majesty steamer Alban, Lt. Tinting, we regret to say, was not sofortunate, althoughequaily deserving ofgood luck, as she grounded in Carlisle bay very soon after the attempt to go away, and now lies fast in the sand. A French barque, Lcs Quatre Ftere, from Cherbourg with mules, put to sea early in the morning, before the gale commenced, and by so doing escaped its fury : the captain of this vessel, it is said, expressed it as his opinion, that a storm of wind was approaching, and hastened away his vessel on that account. Events have justified the opinion. But the picture of distress, although deep in its colouring, yet received an additional gloomy cast, from the number of seamen who formed the crews of the wrecked vessels, and who clinging to the shrouds and sides of their shattered ships for some time supplicated the mercy of the crowds who lined the shore, amid the howling of the winds and the deafening tumults of the waves, but they did not long supplicate in vain. Some more attentive to the calls of humanity than olhers, fearlessly threw aside every consideration of personal

safety and boldly rushed forward into the water to the assistance of their fellow men. Amongst these we have much pleasure in mentioning, Mr. Drinan, Mr Hoytc, and many others, whose names we have not learned, and also a black man of the name of Taylor, who is stower of Cargo Sugar, and by whose intrepidity and dauntless conduct

Tas'iaxrc&usK aa®aa®3ir«3 united with that of others, many of the seamen were safely brought on shore. A most pninful and affecting scene was here exhibited. Of the 0 in crew on board the barque Elizabeth, 2 of them were "boys, and there was also one man who could not swim, how these were to be ianded was the wonder of every one, and the spectators contiguons to the scene, appeared to entertain fears for their lives, presently however, a Life- buoy was rigged out on shore and dispatched to the ship, a thing little kuown here useful as it is upon such occasions, it was drawn up and one of the little fellows w as made fast. The barque at this time was rolling in a swell nearly half as high as her masts, presently over went the boy, iV he was seen no more for some time, ail exclaimed poor fellow, heisgone he is drowned ! when to the great surprise and equal joy of all who witnessed the scene, up came the head of trie buoy and the boy together, he had been dragged all the way beneath the surf, and although hall drowned, was yet alive and was assisted to the land by several of those w ho kept in the water for the purpose, the second boy was rescued from the wreck in the same manner and then the man, but of course the people had now seen the use of a life-buoy, anu they were no longer surprised at its value and ellicacy in preserving iife. His Excellency the Governor with that solicitude which he has ever shewn for the private as well as the public interest of the Island, since his residence amongst us, was at

the spot and in the water, the greater part of the noon, encouraging by persuasions and entreaties those engaged in saving the crews not to relax in their eflorts and we are persuaded the influence of his Excellency's example, lent them both strength and courage in the humane undertaking. Only 3 seamen we believe in the whole have lost their lives, one poor fellow had his skull driven in, by being dashed on the rocks, and died on Wednesday night, and of the other two, one died of exhaustion from chill and cold and the other was drowned, a miraculous preservation of the survivors when it is considered that nearly 200 of these men were exposed to the fury of the storm, on a rocky shore, and the inhabitants to whom they looked for help and protection, in their distressing and forlorn situation, were not one in a thousand, able to assist them for want of proper means, such as ropes, life-boats, buoys, &c. Of the amount of loss sustained by this truly awful and distressing visitation, to the shipping interest, we shall hazard no positive opinion ; as far as appearances go, and according to opinions expressed, we should state it at over one hundred thousand pounds sterling, as most ol the homeward bound vessels were nearly if not fully laden, and the vessels, American and otherwise, discharging their cargoes, had in some instances the greater portion on board. The homeward bound vessels wrecked, are the Corsair with 115 hhds. 17 tierces sugar, and 287 puncheons molasses; Elizabeth 314 hhds.

30 trs. sugar : Pacific, 140 hhds. sugar, 1(50 puns, molasses: Schwartz, 48 hlids. sugar: Sarah Trotman, 339 do ; Britannia, 650 do , 30 trs. ; Harmony, 238 puns, molasses. The situation of the destitue seamen lias naturally excited the commiseration of every portion of the community, and every offer of kindness which humanity could suggest, has been made them. Such of them as had no where to lay their heads, have been comfortably lodged, by order of the Magistrates, in

the different Station Houses, and the merchants interested in the fate of i lie wrecked ships, have paid unremitting attention to their immediate wants, bv furnishing them with new clothsng. A public meeting lias been held, and a handsome sum raised by sub" scriptfon, to enable them to reach their native homes. Upon the land the damage done is comparatively trifling. A few small houses and a paling here and there have been blown down in this town, but nothing beyond this, and in the country the standing corn has been partially stripped, and one or two very high chimneys falling on the buildings to which they were attached, have done partial injury to the roofs.

MAY 31, 1837. the right hon. LORD BEXLEY in the chair. (concluded.) LORD TEIGNMOITTH. þÿ Ladies, and Gentlemen, at this late hour of the day I could willingly have proposed to you this Motion in silence ; but I am perfectly satisfied, that, when you hear it read, von will agree with me, that I should have done justice neither to your feelings nor my own, had I not otlered few words in recommending it to your adoption. It is a motion of cordial thanks to the Noble President of this Institution, for bis obliging conduct in the chair on this occasion. I am sure you will join vviih me in expression of earnest affection and respect to my Noble I' riend, founded on a deep conviction of the importance of the long and laborious services he has rendered to the Institution: and presuming that no individual member of it is more deeply imbued with its þÿspirit the spirit of peace and conciliation, þÿ or more anxious to diffuse that spirit to the utmost limits and through the whole circle of its operations, 1 can assure this meeting 1 am not going to detain them. I shall best consult the feelings of iny Noble Friend, if, instead of dwelling longer on this part of the Motion. 1 advert to the prospect before us þÿ mean, the prospect of renewed exertions, to which we are called by the Report this day. I must also congratulate this Meeting, while surveying the enlarged field that is opened before it that there lias been no former Anniversary of this Society at which a greater number of its Vice- Presidents attended þÿ none, in which the no-
is surrounded, was less broken, ble army, by which your Lordship's or in which a banner greater feeling of unanimity pervaded every part of the Assembly.

BISHOP of þÿCHICHESTER who had returnded in the course of the þÿMeeting I have been requested, very unexpectedly at this late hour, to second the Motion of thanks to the Noble President, for bis attention to the business of the day I confess, there could not have been committed to my charge a task more pleasing to þÿme a task, in which I am quite certain, however feebly I may .execute it, I shall carry with me the approbation of this Meeting. 1 cannot help remembering þÿ it is now, I believe, more than thirty years ago þÿ how much this Society was first indebted to the promptitude and intelligence with which it was taken up and supported by our Noble President At that time it consisted of, I may say, so few persons, that, I believe, we might all have met in an upper chamber : and, My Lord, though, at that time, there were many persons among us of young anil buoyant feelings, who were tempted to speculate very largely on the success which would one day accompany this Society, I believe it never entered into the mind of the

most sanguine to imagine the degree of success which has been granted to it þÿ to imagine that it should have been, within thirty years, celebrated by such an Assembly as this that þÿ its labours should have been carried to such an extent, through every quarter of the world þÿ and that we should have, on this occasion, to hear of Assemblies which are about to meet in another quarter of the globe, to support the liible Society, which may, perhaps, be as numerous as this which we now behold. My Lord, I am very well aware that all present considerations are as nothing, in comparison with the great object which ought to occupy our hearts þÿ the propagation of the Gospel : but if there be a person to whom, in my mind, this Society is indebted more than another, it is our Noble President It was at the bright flame of his charity that my taper was first lighted ; and I am sure that it is a gratification jto every one of us who are present, that that flame of charity has burnt, with him, as brightly and steadily as it did at first, until the present day. I am sure that it is no small gratification to him, that the great importance that attached to his support at that moment is of little value now ; and that the light which he then spread around us in so many quarters, and wdiicli shed so much happiness on the Society, requires no aid now from any individual whatever, but depends on an aft'ection which, 1 trust, can never pass away. I ought here, perhaps, to close what I have

to offer ; but there is one point which has been touched upon in your Report, on which I feel a sort of impulse to say a few words to you : that is, the disquietudes which have been expressed respecting certain very agitating and exciting questions, which are on the public mind in the present day þÿ as if it were a prospect unfavourable to this Society. Now 1 remember, that when, with our Noble President and many others, 1 assisted, feebly indeed, in the support of this Society, one great argument we held forth was, that this Society would be the means of uniting in Christian love, Dissenters, and Members of the Church of England ; and I would appeal to all who are present þÿ 1 would appeal to your own hearts, and to the history of times past þÿ whether the prediction lias not been verified" Whatever differences may have existed, or do exist, in the political world þÿ whatever resentments may exist in many minds at this very moment, or excitements, I should rather say þÿ for I hope resentment there is none ; but, whatever excitements there may be, there would have been many more, but for this Society. And why then, 1 ask, should the Society cease to operate, in the same manner that it has done ? I see no reason : and my opinion is, that, instead of the Society's having any thing to dread from these excitements, the excitements themselves will be exceedingly softened, and the bad effects of them much diminished, by the very sense which we all entertain of that love which we ought to bear to each other þÿ of

that legacy wiiich the Saviour bequeathed to His Disciples þÿ and of that mark which He has impressed oil us þÿ the mark of Christian peace and love. I trust, therefore, my Christian friends, that you will not be satisfied þÿ I speak to Churchmen as well as to Dissenters þÿ with divesting your minds, in this place, of all irritable feelings with respect to the questions of which I speak : but that, when you go away, you will determine, in your own hearts, that your co-operation in this noble Christian work shall be the means of softening feelings, which might otherwise have arisen in your minds, of an exciting kind, and preventing them from having any effect on that peace of society around yon, which is of so much importance to every good work and every good feeling þÿ but particularly to the success of that Society, which we arc now met. to advocate and support. With this wish þÿ with this prayer, 1 will say þÿ deeply, strongly impressed on your minds, I would advise jyou to depart, and let us close the Meeting with this prayer. 1 will also add a prayer, that when your President, to whom you give your thanks this day, shall depart from this life þÿ which he will not do, 1 trust, for the sake of the Society, for many years þÿ he may depart in peace, with the convictiou

that no interruption has taken place to prevent the complete success of the Society ; but that it is growing still in the approbation of men's minds, and propagating Christian faith and charity throughout the whole world.

EARL OF CHICHESTER þÿ Ladies and Gentlemen, As the Motion, which has just been moved and seconded, cannot be put from the chair, my Reverend friend, the Se cretary, has requested me to propose it to you. I know not why my esteemed 'friend has selected me for this duly, unless from a feeling that he could not have chosen one who would be more sure not to inflict on thi3 Meeting another speech: or because he knew, as 1 am sure he does, that there is not one who feels a more cordial personal respect and affection for our Noble President than rryself; or, 1 hope I may also add, a more earnest desire, arising from a sense of paramount obligation, to support, to the best of my power, that great Society over which his Lordship presides.

LORD BEX þÿLEY. Ladies and Gentlemen, 1 have, from year to year, increasing cause to feel the partial kindness of the friends whom 1 see around me : on this occasion friend, tlie Right Reverend Prelate, particularly, I must beg to allude who to my has so feelingly referred to the situation which I have had the honour to hold in this Society, though the circumstances of it have been much exaggerated by bis kind partiality. I beg you to believe that I have ever been sincerely attached to the Society ; though 1 feel how inefficient my service has been ; and that, from the age to which I have lived, 1 shall be front year to year more indebted to your indulgence, if any future approbation should be given to the service 1 perform. So long as health and strength are allotted me by the Most High, it will be my highest gratification to devote them to the Society. þÿ From year to year, I feel my attachment to it growing and increasing: and on no account more, than from a conviction that this Society, united in Christian love for the diffusion of the Gospel ; is beyond any other Institution, calculated for the promotion of Christian charity, for the removal of prejudices, partialities, and differences of opinion, and for uniting us all in the Truth. 1 take my leave of you, with a renewed and inci eased sense of your kindness.

Apple Bread. þÿ A Frcncli officer has invented, and practised with great success, a method of making bread with common apples, very far superior to potato bread. Alter having boiled one-third of peeled apples, be bruised them while quite warm into two thiuls of flour, including the proper quantity of yeast, and kneaded the whole without water, the juice of the fruit being quite sufficient \\ hen this mixture had acquired the consistency of paste, he put it into a vessel, in which he allowed it to rise for about twelve hours. By this process he obtained a very excellent bread, full of eyes, and extremely palatable and light. þÿ Doctor.

ILLUMINATED FEINTING. In many of tlie old printed books, the initial letters, and occasionally other parts, were printed in red. This was done by two workings at press, and was an imitation of the earlier fashion of illuminating manuscripts. þÿ The practice is still followed in some almanacks, the Saints days and holy days being " red letter days." Some ingenious contrivances have been devised for working in various colours, and very recently printing in gold and other metals has been practised. Some very handsome specimens of this have been produced by a printer of this town (who can, we understand, supply his typographical brethren among the islands with a few ounces of each color, five in number) ; but of course the price is too costly ever to enter into competion with common printing, or to be used for other than purposes of ornament. þÿ Barbados Mercury.

THE BLACKSMITHS BOTTLE A blacksmith, in extensive business, had a bottle that held exactly a pint, and in the large village where he resided, it was soon known in its various trips to the stores as an exact guagc for that quantity, and on its appearance for replenishing, was filled without recourse to the measure. This bottle became celebrated. Eighteen years it performed the drudgery of being the medium of conveying the ruinous beverage to the owner and his workmen. During this long course of service, the shop in which it was so conspicuous an appendage, was several times consumed by fire, but eacli time the bottle was found among the ruins uninjured Phcenix-like it rose, and was taken again into active service. It was kept in motion like a weaver's shuttle ; and such zealous devotcrs, at the bacchanalian altar, vvere its possessors, that it has been known to convey fourteen shillings worth of the poison in a single day to the occupants of the shop. The bottle has survived its owner, who has recently passed into the grave at the age of sixty, a veteran toper : although he originally possessed a constitution, that, under different habits, promised to carry him to the period attained by many a temperate pilgrim, that of eighty years or more þÿ and instead of competence to his survivors, has left the little bottle, emptied of its contents, as their only legacy. This veteran bottle has been the medium of conveying more wealth from its owner and his workmen, than would have sufficed to purchase

the most extensive and valuable farm the country can boast of. As well might Jthe occupants of the shop have heaped up coals on their forge and put their utmost exertions in exercise upon their bellows to put out the fire, as to undertake to quench alcoholic thirst with ardent spirits. The more frequent the recurrence to the little bottle for supplies, the more powerful is the desire to embrace it again and again ; and the more frequent the embrace, the greater and more certain the necessity of return. Are there not many more Utile bottles that are conveying the wealth, by daily, small, certain, and sure steps, out of the possession of the owners, and pouring into their systems a tide of ruin which will never cease to flow, and which will finally overwhelm them in a destruction that has cternily for its duration ? shirt tree. The numerous and well-known voyages to the South Sea islands, Ac., have made us all well acquainted with what is called the breadtree, as well as another kind known under the name of the butter-tree. But it remained for the indefatigable M. Humboldt to discover in the wilds of South America, a tree which produces ready-made shirts. W e saw on " the slope of the (Jena Dnida," says M. Humboldt, " shirt-tress fifty feet high. The Indians cut off' cylindrical pieces two feet in diameter, from which they peel the red and fibrous bark, without making any longitudinal incision. This bark, affords them a sort of garment, which resembles sacks of a very coarse texture, and without a seam. The upper opening serves lor the head, and two lateral holes are cut to admit the arms. The natives wear these shirts of marima in the rainy season : they have the form of the ponchos and ruanos of cotton, which are so common in New Grenada, at Quito, and in Peru. As in those climates the riches and beneficence of nature arc regarded as the primary causes of the indolence of the inhabitants, the missionaries do not fail to say >n showing the shirts of marima, ' in the forests of the Oroonoko, garments are found ready made on the trees.' We may add to this tale of the shirts, the pointed caps, which the spathes of certain palm-trees furnish, and which resemble coarse network." þÿ Tilloch's Mag.

Extraordinary Fact. þÿ It was Dr. Currie, the accomplished biographer of Burns, who first recommended cold immersion in cases of fever, more particularly where the type takes the name of scarlet. The suggestion, we believe, proved not a little startling, and the public naturally enough revolted at the idea of tearing a patient from bis warm bed, and plunging him suddenly into a cold bath, whether under cover or in the open air. But the practice gained ground notwithstanding, and many striking recoveries were accomplished by a remedy, which to many seemed worse than the disease, or, at all events more likely to kill than to cure. Still so peculiar a mode of treatment required the greatest delicacy on the part of the practitioner, and, though not of the faculty, we have always understood that it was only in a certain crititical stage of the disease that Dr. Currie himself considered it safe or advisable to hazard the experiment. Accordingly, the practice has been discontinued. From the aversion which patients and relatives so generally cherish to so rough a trial, and farther, from the opinion that copious sponging serves all the purposes of the cold bath. Jn this opinion, wc confess we do not entirely agree ; but, be that as it may, wc proceed to record tho following very curious fact: þÿ A young man, residing in Castle- Douglas, (whose name will be given privately il required,) had, while la-

AVSSU bouring under influenza, accompanied or followed by typhus fever, become so delirious that his friends found it necessary to watch him closely. From some accident, however, his attendants, for a brief space, were out of the way on Tuesday week, the 22d curt, and on that day the patient rose from bed, and with no other clothing save his night-cap and shirt, actually walked to the Carlinwark loch, bathed, and returned home in the same state he went. Going and returning, the distance is, as near as may be, half a-mile, and it will be recollected that Tuesday was a bitter day, with severe frost in the valleys and snow upon the hills. On reaching his father's house he was immediately put to the bed, and, strange as it may appear, soon after became calm and collected. The fever too, abated, and on Saturday last, when a friend wrote to us, he was still improving to such a degree as to induce the hope of speedily convalescenc e.-Dumfries Courier.

BARBADOS. From the NEW TIMES, July 28. We were visited again, by the permission of an all- wise Providence, on the 26th, by a gale of wind so violent in its commencement as to lead us to expect nothing less than an awful repitition of the Hurricane of 31 þÿ During the gale, dependent on that Providence, and utterly helpless in ourselves ; feeling too our nothingness, and that we were but as mere reptiles of the earth, conscious of our sins, and ingratitude, what could we feel, than what we did feel ! þÿ We asked not frail man, like ourselves, tho' rich and dignified with titles, to bespeak our feelings : þÿ God knew them ! and that was enough ! þÿ We have every reason to bend our knees in reverence and give our whole heart in deep gratitude to him, that our fearful expectations were not realized. He knows what we can bear and he will never impose a burden. that his children cannot sustain Oh ! would that we were but half as loyal to Him our heavenly, as to our terrestrial Sovereign ! What rebels, ingrates are we ! 1 ! However, He the Almighty arrested the fury of the Elements, and here we are to praise his unmerited goodness. We have as yet learned, that the Country has comparatively suffered little. Thanks be to God alone ! 1 The shipping tho' has materially We lament it from the bottom of our hearts and can only say, : that we must humbly submit, as God, the Omnipotent, the sustainer of all things sent the affliction. A description of the loss of Vessels dzc. will be given from the Columns of our Cotempora-

ries, and in allusion to our Cotemporaries, we will not, we cannot, omit the mention of the noble conduct of His Excellency the Governor, Sir E. MacGregor, and the Editor of the Globe, Andrew Drinan, Esq., þÿ in his strenuous endeavours to save from Fire and Water as many of his fellow sufferers as he could ; and in many instances, his humane feelings were gratified. We regret extremely to announce that the ship Britannia, one of the five vessels which rode out the hurricane at her anchors þÿ with the loss of her mizen-mast, has sustained so much injury that she will probably have to be enumerated amongst the victims of the gale. Crowds were employed until nearly one þÿo clock on Thursday, endeavouring to get out her cargo of Sugar, but she was then found to be making water so fast, (four feet nine inches in the hour) that the Steamer City of Kingston was employed to tow her to the head of the Pay, where she was beached, to prevent her sinking at her moorings. Her þÿMajesty s ship Gannct was moored with four anchors, but she drew them all, and had the gale lasted one hour longer, she must have shared the common fate, notwithstanding that all her masts were struck at an early hour, and that she looks to be an excellent sea boat. The Ship Fortitude, tho moored in ten fathom water, and held to the last by her anchors, is reported to have struck once, and injured her rudder and stern post. At five o'clock in the morning the wind was quite moderate, and the sea considerably gone
down ; but these elements had wrought their work of desolation, and done injury to the Shipping and their Cargoes which will scarcely be covered by £100,000 sterling ! 1 !

THE QUEEN OF ENGLAND. She is said to be a young lady of much excellence of disposition, of much natural discernment, and, what is inestimable when accompanied by good sense, much of that strength and firmness of character which eminently distinguished, in the brightest periods of his life, one of her illustrious ancestors, who sat upon the throne of England þÿ we mean the paternal grandfather of her Royal Highness the upright and unbending þÿ George the Third. How far the native endowments of the Young Queen may have been improved by a judicious and generous culture, it is not for us to pronounce. We are bound to hope that those who were either nominally entrusted with the education of a young personage destined to fill a situation so exalted, and, what is a subject of far wider interest, to dis charge functions so grave and manifold, and so sustain a responsibility so awful, or if not the nominal depositories of such a trust, we are to hope, at least that those who may have substantially superseded them in their office, and taken, upon themselves the practical communication to her youthful mind of that 1 amount of some bills he got cashed, he and knowledge by which it ought to have been deligently furnished, and of those various ha- 1 affairs. They gave out that he had a most bits and attainments which are not ornamental merely, but indispensable to him or her who wears a crown þÿ we must hope, we say that those persons whoever they were, may have endeavoured conscientiously to stamp upon her heart not alone the feminine, but the

Royal virtues, and to have opened the spirit of the future Queen of England to the breadth and grandeur of her last approaching obligations, political as well as moral. In referring to that course of bringing up which would be best adapted to the formation of a British Sovereign, beg we to disclaim all design whatever of insinuating, as a matter of fact, that justice has not been rendered to her Majesty by those from whom her Majesty had the most undoubted right to demand it. We do devoutly pray that those persons may be found to have conducted her education and as an essential portion of it, her intercourse with society, under a noble and lofty regard to her firmness for the duties of a Queen of England apart from all mean and selfish considerations of what might most contribute, by and by to their own aggrandizement or indulgence. It is manifest that the same attainments which might tend to make an accomplished woman in private life must be wholly insufficient for a Queen Regent of Great Britain. A person of her illustrious rank and trying functions ought to be prepared in early life to think for herself, to form under difficult circumstances, prompt & independent resolutions þÿ to employ her own discernment upon the characters of all around her þÿ to take nothing upon trust ; she ought to be influenced by her elders through reason rather than coercion to be taught how to detect the deceitful, to keep the presumptious aloof, to hold intriguers in abhorrence. She ought to be treat-

ed even, while a child with an eye to her early maturity. Above all this, she ought not, alter approach to womanhood, to have been made the subject of jealous and vexatious restraints, or continued in a state of narrow pupilage after she had reached that position wherein she might be called upon for the exercise of a responsible will, of a disciplined judgment, and an enlarged intelligence.

She has a mighty but honest and tolerant people to propitiate. She will justify the historian in recording that the British monarchy has perished with William IV., or that the best interest of the reformed religion throughout this realm have by the successor of King William been abandoned and betrayed. A Good and True Joke. þÿ For some months past a person residing in the town of Armagh contrived to do an extensive business with the Agricultural Bank, but finding that the firm proposed coming down on him for the

his wife adopted a novel plan for settling his maglignant fever, and in three days after he expired. A coffin was piocured, and filled not with the remains of poor John, but with mother earth, and word being sent to the priest that he would be interred at two þÿo clock, his reverence attended, and having to all appearance buried poor John, collected £7 of offerings þÿ the disconsolate widow, having a little property left belonging to her greatly regretted husband, actually administered, and from the pitiful story she made, the gentlemen concerned in executing the administration not only gave their services gratis, but also raised some money for her, as poor John was a general favourite. A gentleman belonging to Armagh happened to be in Liverpool about three weeks ago, and to his great surprise and terror observed poor John a short distance before him. Having summoned up sufficient courage he went up to him ; John at first denied he was the person, but on finding the gentleman would not be further imposed on, he confessed all, and promised to pay as soon as able. When the gentleman came home he went to the widow, and asked had he retuined from Liverpool, on which she got very angry, asserting that her poor husband had died of two days illness. The gentleman persevering in his assertion, the widow said if he was seen it must have been his ghost. Beet root Sugar. þÿ Such are the great improvements introduced of late by the practical chemists of France þÿ such as the Says and the Delesscrts þÿ into the crystallization ol the juice ol the beet, that in several ot the great manufactories the domestic produce is preferred to the transatlantic muscovado for the purposes of the relincr. In this happy result all true philantropists must rejoice, inasmuch as the culture of the sugar cane, as long as its produce continues an indispensable item of European consumption, must tend to perpetuate negro slavery, and to operate as a premium on the atrocious traffic in human flesh. The attention of Germany and of the United States of America, has also been attracted to a subject in which the interests of trade and humanity are fortunately found to afford each other mutual support. From our Paris correspondent we learn that several missionaries had arrived in France, from the United Stales, for the purpose of studying the practical culture of the beet, and the profitable application of its various pioducts, of which sugar is, of course, by far the most important, although modern chemistry has taught the means of converting the refuge to most valuable uses. During the present season large tracts of land in the states of Ohio and Illinois, Alabama and Indiana, have been sown with the seed of the Silesian beet imported from Europe ; and numerous specimens of the simple instruments employed in French Flanders and Belgium, and especially in the Grand

Duchy of Nassau, have been sent out to i he free settlers in the far west, for the purpose of enabling them, where manual labour is so expensive, to produce sugar so cheaply as to compete successively with that produced in the slave-holding states of the south, abolishing the premium on the further importation of negroes, and depriving the lash of the slavedriver of its incentive and its charm. þÿ Morning paper.

Orange Rind. þÿ The ripe fruit of the sweet orange is useful either from its rind or its acid juice. The rind is ordered in some pharmacopoeias, though not in that of London. It is a mild tonic and aromatic, principally used for its flavour þÿ Large þÿquantities, says the editor of the United States Dispensatory, þÿ are sometimes productive of mischief, especially in children, in whom colic and even convulsions, are sometimes induced by it. þÿ We have known the case of a child, in which death resulted from eating the rind of an orange þÿ A very fragrant oil (the essential of sweet orange of the perfumer) is obtained from the outer rind þÿ 1 Medical Gazette.

The Spey Packet, conveying the Mails to Europe, likewise brought the 1st July mails, conveyed to Barbados by the Lyra. þÿ The intelligence by them confirms the report of the deatli of his Majesty, WILLIAM IV, which event took place on the morning of the 20th June at Windsor Castle, þÿ evidently to the great regret and sorrow of all classes of his þÿMajesty subjects s ; indeed, from a perusal of the English papers, it would seem that few sovereigns who have swayed the sceptre of Great Britain have been more deservedly lamented. The young Queen Victoria seen.s already to have gained golden opinions from all parties, if we may judge from the speeches of the leaders of the two great conflicting parties in Parliament. þÿ Hung be the heavens with black, yield to day and night, Comets importingchange of times and states, Brandish your crystal tresses in the sky ; And with them scourge the bad revolting stars, That have consented unto Williams death! William the fourth too famous to live long! England ne'erlost a King of so much þÿworth. Shakespeare. Alas! the dreadful news is true ! ! William the fourth our beloved Monarch is gathered to his fathers þÿ and though on the arrival of the Packet, the newspapers were most anxiously opened, and read, yet something more was still expected, every countenance exhibited something which will be easier conceived than expressed. þÿ It is not in our power on this melancholy occasion to indulge in the language of pancgeric, or to con-

fine ourselves within the mere ordinary bounds of loyal and enthusiastic condolence þÿ those who are, or have been bound to others by the silken bands of friendship, are not strangers to that finest and noblest feelings of social sympathy'. þÿ Alas; what forlorn dread steals þÿo er the spirit of man, when the solemn funeral knell reverberating as it were thro' his inmost soul, and awakens him to the conscious reflection that the corpse of a play-fel low, a boon companion, or a sincere friend is about to be laid below, in that cold solitary grave, which for ever cuts off a segment of that little circle which a few revolving years at farthest will entirely obliterate from the sphere of existence þÿ but sudden yet, and far more sudden it is to reflect, that the Venerable companion and friend of our dear parents, hath now breathed his last þÿ King William the Fourth of England was once well known in this Island, and though few remain to tell how the hospitable sons of little Nevis entertained their Royal Prince, yet there are eyes still undimned at this very spot which once gazed on the brilliant countenance of youthful Royally. þÿ Ves, a few still remain to shed the tear of unfeigned grief for their late Royal master, and the sons and daughters of Roy al þÿWilliam friends s have truly mourned for iiim who was doubly dear to them. When the Packet arrived, His Honor the President was at his country seat, a messenger in great haste was immediately posted off, and in a surprising short space of time, His

þÿHonor carriage s was in tow; but as Saturday was the day of Militia meeting, and also the sitting day of the Special Magistrate, and alþÿtho the hours of business terminated at 12 o'clock, yet the multiplicity of complaints (owing perhaps to the sitting days being reduced to 2 per week) caused the lower hall

At half past 1 þÿo clock in the afternoon the Provost Marshal repaired to the Court House to prepare for the reception of His Honor the President, and in the space of eight minutes alter his þÿHonor Carriage s drawn by a splendid pair of light bays made its appearance ; all was then tranquility ; and þÿaltlio Saturday was a market day, and the square in front of the Court House was crowded with apprentice labourers from the country, as well as persons of every deseiiption, yet solemn silence reigned over all, and the whole mass of human beings appeared as if they had been represented in one vast drawing. When his Honor arrived at the Council Chamber, the Provost Marshal assembled all the principal inhabitants, and never shall we forget that distress which clouded the aspect of all present, and when the Despatch containing King þÿWilliam decease, s and Queen Victoria's proclamation was read from President Daniei.l, down to the humblest individual, every one appeared as if he had just heard of the death of his dearest, and nearest relation, and even when Her Royal Highness was proclaimed, þÿ þÿ Gou Save the Queen" was responded in a melancholy tone ; the hi st ey e that beamed joy after was President Dameli.'s, who looking on Her þÿMajesty s signature, exclaimed, þÿ behold the beautiful signature of our handsome, and accomplished

young Queen." The effect produced by these words was perfectly astonishing þÿ the radiant balo of the brilliant star of Brunswick, seemed at that moment to have been present to lighten up every countenance, we lelt ourselves lost in amazement whilst contemplating the scene then before us, but our sole attention was soon fixed on the Venerable Lawyer, whose pilgrimage in this life of trouble and vexation has already exceeded fourscore years, who seemed in that moment of surpassing joy to forget the rush of rolling years, which had thinned his silvery locks, þÿ Upon the whole the scene was such as baffles description þÿ it was mourning mixed with joy. In conclusion, we beg leave to express our highest approbation of the zeal, aflection and loyalty ol the people Nevis; Heaven grant of them prosperity and happiness under tlie golden sceptre of Queen Victoria.

Malibran. þÿ This lamented songstress is thus noticed in a new work entitled the þÿ Victims of þÿSociety, by the countess of Bless ington : The only amusements I enjoy in London a e the theatres and the opera One of the divine þÿShakespeare t s ragedies, with Macready to personate the chief character, can always charm me ; and at such representations I forget my chagrin and my self. 1 have always had, as you know, an inordinate passion for music ; jbut it has greatly increased since 1 have been accustomed to listen to the heartstirring voice of the inspired Malibran, or the dulcet tones of la Grisi. The first inimitable songstress draws me continually to Drury lane, where she is engaged, and it seems tome that I listen with increased delight to her the more I become acquainted with the power and pathos of hor voice. The low notes of it produce nri eflcct on me that no other's ever did. The sound appears to emanate from u soul thrilling with

atis ; MmMWHiHWþÿf w am sublime emotions, þÿ andits deep harmony causes mine to vibrate. There is something mysterious, something magical in its influence on me. It haunts me for many succeeding hours, and seems to me as if it arose from an inspired, passionate and despairing heart, in an intensely profound consciousness of the insufficiency of mortal powers to satisfy' the aspirations of an immortal spirit to a release from its earthly trammels, and to the fulfilment of a wider and nobler destiny I have avoided becoming personally acquainted with Malibran, because, I am told, she is the most animated and gay person imaginable, giving utterance to the liveliest sallies and most native observations. For this peculiarity, which draws a flattering homage around her, I shun her society ; because 1 would not have the associations with w hich she is mingled in my mind disturbed by a light word or heartless jest, from lips that seem to me only formed for the creation of the most sublime sounds Those deep eyes of hers, too, have a profound melancholy, even in their flashing lustre; and 1 have never so perfect a sympathy with my compatriots as when 1 hear those divine notes of hers followed by the plaudits of hundreds, too enthusiastically expressed to leave a doubt of the sincerity of the heartfelt admiration that excites them. Malibran, in my opinion, seems to inspire her audience : they are no lopgcr a vast crowd assembled to be amused ; no, they assume a much more imposing aspect : thev are carried away by passionate emotion, by

generous impulses, and feel within themselves capabilities, of Mie existence of which they were previously ignorant. She ceases to be a mere singer, or paid actress, in their eyes ; she becomes an inspired sibyl, that reve als to them gleams of a purer, brighter wot Id, which they had forgotten, but to which her divine tones summon them to return.

But beware, vc Lady Loritncrs ' these lovers of peace and quiet, these managed husbands, are the very men to abuse their liberty, if once they get it. I would rather trust the man who roves where he will, when he will, fearless alike of his w ife & her frowns, than one of those cooped up men, who like the canary, if once his cage door be opened, flies <.(f in the full enjoyment and in the full abuse of the liberty ol which lie has been so long deprived. The dying þÿman. It is a very terrible and amazing thing to see a man die, and solemnly j take his last leave of the world The very circumstances of dying men are apt to strike us with horror To hear such a man, how sensibly he will speak of the other world, as if lie were just come from it, rather than going to it; how severely he wil! condemn himself for the folly and wickedness of his lilc ; with what passion he will wish that he had lived better, and had served God more sincerely . how seriously he will resolve upon a better life, if God would be pleased to raise him up, and try him once more ; with what z.eal and earnestness he will commend to his best friends and nearest relations a religious and virtuous course of life, as the only thing that will minister comfort to them when they come to be in his condition. Such discourses as these are very apt to move and alleci men for tho time, and to stir up in them very good resolutions, whilst the present lit and impression lasts; but because these sights are very frequent, they have seldom any great permanent effect upon men. They consider that it is a very common case, and sinners take example and encouragement from one another ; every one is afleeted for the present, few are so effectually convinced as to betake themselves to a better course. þÿ Tillotson.

" Sir 1" cried Charnev, " behold in good time a new text enabling you to enlarge upon the mysteries of creation," Girardi took the insect with due precaution; examined it carefully ; paused for reflection ; and suddenly an expression of triumph developed itself in his countenance An irresistible argument seemed to have fallen from heaven into his hands Commencing in his usual professional tone he gradually assumed a more sublime expression, as the secret object of his lesson penetrated through his Ian" guage. " Mere-fly-catcher as I am," he began, with an arch smile, " I must restrict myself to my humble attributions, and not presume to affect the pedantry of the scholar." " The most enlightened mind," said Charney, " the mind which has profited most largely by the acquirement knowledge, is of that which soonest discovers the limitation of its own powers, after vainly attempting to penetrate into the hidden mysteries of things. Genius itself breaks its wings against such obstacles, without having extracted from the wall of flints, by which it is obstructed, one spark of the light of truth " « We ignoramuses," observed Girardi, "arrive sooner at our object, by taking the most direct road. If we do but open our eyes, God deigns to reveal himself in the august

sublimity of his works." " On that point, we are agreed," interrupted Charney. " Proceed we then in our course. An herb of the field srffieed to prove to you tin1 existence of a Providence, a butterfly, the law of universal harmony ; the insect before us, of which the organization is of a still higher order, may lead us still further towards conviction " Charney, at the instance of his friend, proceeded to examine the little stranger with -urious attention. Behold this insignificant creature," resumed Girardi. " All that hntnan genius could effect would not add one title to organization perfectly adapted to its wants and necessities. It has wings to transpo. i it from one place to another ; elytra to one tse and 3ecure them from the contact of any hard substance. Its breast is defended by a cuirass, its eyes by a curious network, that defies tlie prick of a thorn or the sting of an enemy. It possesses antennae to interrogate the obstacles that present themselves, feet to attain its prey, iron manditdes to assist in devouring it, in digging the earth for a refuge, or a depository for its food or eggs, if a dangerous adversary should approach, it has in reserve an acrid and corrosive fluid, by discharging which it defies its enemies. Instinct teaches it to find its lood, to provide its lodging, and exercise its powers of offence and defence. þÿ Nor this a solitary instance. Other insects is are endowed with similar delicacy of organization The imagination recoils with wonder
from the multiplicity and variety of provisions invented by nature for the security of the apparently feeble jnscct tribes. We have still to consider this fragile creature as demon-

TasT-mxt'JtsK saiMtatitiiiras ATIS. w - .jrnum iqio WK i . . þÿ þÿMaKfcaMVM i. þÿw þÿM þÿw þÿ strating the line of demacration between man kind and the brute creation. " Man is sent naked into the world, feeble helpless, unendowed with the wings of the bird, the swiftness of the stag, the tortuous speed ot the serpent; without means of defence against the c.laws or darts of an enemy, nay, against even the inclemency ol the weather. lie has no shell, no fleece, no covering ot fur ; nor even a den or burrow for his hiding piace. Yet by force of his natural powers, he has driven the lion from his cave, despoiled the bear of his shaggy coat for a vestment, and the bull of his horn to form a drinking cup He has dug into the entraiis of the earth, to bring forth elements of future strength ; the very eagle, in traversing the skies, finds himself struck down in the midst of its career to adorn his cup with a trophy of distinction. "Which of all the animal creation could have supported itself in the midst of such difficulties and such privations? Let us suppose for a moment the disunion of power and action, of God and nature. Nature has done wonders for the insect before us : for man, apparently nothing. Because man, an emanation from God himself and formed alter his image, was created feeble and helpless as regards the organization of matter, tn order to demonstrate the divine influence of that etlierial spark, which endows him with all the elements of future greatness."

" Explain to me, at least," interrupted Charney, the peculiar value of this precious gift, bestowed, you say, exclusively upon the human species ; superiot in many points to tne animal creation, surely we are inferior in the majority, This very insect, whose wondrous powers you have expounded, inspires me with a sense of inferiority and profound humiliation." " From time immemorial," replied Girardi, " animals have displayed no progress in their powers of operation. What they ate to day, such have they ever been ; what to-day they know, they have known fiom the beginning ol the world. 11 born so lavishly endowed, it is because they arc incapable of improvement. They live not by their own wtii, but by the impulse imparted to them by nature. From the creation until now, the heaver has constructed his lodge upon the same plan ; the culterpiliar and spider woven their cocoons and tissues of the same form : the bee projected his cell of the same hexagon ; the lionant traced without a compass its circles and arches. The character of llieir labours is thai of exactitude and uniformity ; that of man, diversity ; for human labour arises from a free and creative faculty of mind. Judge, therefore, between them ! Of all created beings, man alone -possesses the idea of duty, of responsibility, of contemplation, of piety. þÿ Alone of all the earth lie is endowed with insight into futurity, and the knowledge of life and death." " But is this knowledge an advantage ; is it a source of happiness ?" demanded the

Count. " Why has God bestowed upon us reason by which we are led astray, and learning which serves but to perplex us? With all our superiority iiow often are we forced to despise ourselves 1 Why is the exclusively privileged being the only one liable to error ? Is not the instinct of animals preferable to our glimmering reason ?" " Both species were not created for the same end. God requires not virtue of the brute creation. Were they endowed with reason, with liberty of choice as regards their

þÿ food and lodgment, the equilibrium of the world would be destroyed The will of the Creator decided, that the surface of 1 he globe, and even its depths, should be filled with animated beings : that life should pervade the universe ; in pursuance of which, plains, valleys, forests, from the mountain top to the lowest chasm, þÿ trees, rocks, rivers, lakes, oceans, from the sandy desert to the marshy swamp: in all climates and lattitudes ; from one pole to the other ; all is peopled, all instinct with life, all blended in one vast sphere of existence. Whether sheltered in the depths of the wilderness or behind a blade of grass, the lion and the pismire are alike at their post assigned them by nature. Each has his part to play, his place to guard, his predestined line of action ; each is enchained within its proper bound ; for every square of the infinite chessboard was from the first appropriately filled. Man alone is free to range over all ; to traverse eceans and deserts ; pitch his tent on the sand, or construct a floating palace on the waters, to defy the Alpine snows or the fervours of the torrid zone ; " The world is all before bim, where to choose His place of rest, and providence his guide:" " But, if Providence indeed exert such influence, from whence the crimes arising in all human communities, and the disasters which overwhelm mankind ?" cried Charney. " I sympathize in your admiration of ali created things; my reason is overwhelmed when 1 examine the mighty whole, but on descend- "

ing " to the history of the human species þÿ My friend," interrupted Girardi, " arraign not the wisdom of the Almighty because of the errors of mankind, the devastations of a hurricane, or the eruptions of a volcano ' Immutable laws are imprinted upon matter, and the work of ages is accomplished, whether a vessel founder in a storm, or a city disappear beneath the surface of the þÿearth. Of what account in the sight o of the a Almitrhtv c J a few human existences more or less ? Does the Supreme Being believe in the reality of death, the darkness of the grave? " No! But He has conferred on our souls the power of self government, and this is proved by the independence of our passions. I have portrayed animals submitted to the irresistible influence of instinct, possessing only blind tendencies, and the qualities inherent in their several species. Man alone is the parent of his virtues and his vices; man alone is endowed ,with free agency ; because for him this earth is a place of probation. þÿ The tree of good and evil which we cultivate here, is to bear its fruits in a higher or a lower region. Do you imagine the Omniscient God so unjust as to leave the afflictions of the virtuous unrewarded? Were; Were this world the limit of our reward and punishment, the man who dies by a stroke of lightning ought to be counted a malefactor, and the fortune of the prosperous should suffice as a certification of excellence !" Charney listened insilcnce : impressed by the simple eloquence of his instructor, his

eyes were fixed upon the noble countenance on which the excitement of a mind innately pious was imprinting an almost august character of inspiration " But why," at length murmured the Count, " why has not God vouchsafed us the positive certainty of our immortality?" " Doubt was perhaps, indispensable," replied the venerable man, rising and placing his hand affectionately on the shoulder ol his youthful companion, "to repress the vanity ol human reason. What is the merit ol vbr-

tue, if its rewards be assured beforehand ? þÿ Whit would become of free will ? The soul of man is expansive, but not infinite ; vast in its power of apprehending its own distinctions and of appreciating the Creator by the mightiness of his works ; yet so limited as to render it profoundly sensible of its dependance upon Providence. Man is permitted a glimpse of his destinies þÿ Faith must effect the rest. " Oh ! mighty and all-seeing God" cried Girardi, suddenly interrupting himself, and clasping his hands in all the fervour of supplication, " lend me the strength of thine arm to upraise from the dust this man who is struggling with his human weakness and the desire to reach thy fountains of light ! Lend mc thy wisdom to direct the aspirations of this longing and bewildered soul I Lend eloquence to the words of my lips, that they may be endued .villi the strength and power of the faith that i in me ! The humblest of thy creations, a flower, and an insect, have startled the sceptic in ins self security ; give grace to these, O lord I if not to me, to perfect the work thine infinite mercy has begun: and if not by me, : v the humble plant before us, be the miracle of thy holiness accomplished !" The old man was silent. St. Croix, CHRISTIANSTED, ( THURSDA Y) August 31, 1837. By the 2nd July packet we have London dates of the 15 th ultimo, hut the papers art unusually barren of interesting intelligence. The late King's funeral took place on the 8lh July at Windsor ; and was attended with the same pageantry, ceremonies, and parade as were observed at the funeral of Geo: ge 4th. The London papers are full of addresses of the candidates for seals in the house of Commons, to their constituents, preparatory to the new election. Parliament was expected to be dissolved on the 20th July, and a new one summoned to meet early in November þÿ both parties are sanguine of success; but from the great monied power of the conservative party, their union, and influence, the chances are in their favor þÿ the Liberal parly ate much divided, being formed of three distinct parties, whigs, radicals and O'Connellites, who differ from each other strongly in their principles. þÿ Lord Durham has published a letter, the object o f which appears to be to repudiate the current opinion, that he advocates radical principles, þÿ no mention is made of his being about to enter the cabinet, nor will their probably be any change made in the ministry until after the Parliamentary election. Don Carlos has again out manoeuvred his opponents, having crossed the Ebro on the 2'.Hh June near Tortosa, formed a junction with Cabrera, and it is said he, has taken Valencia; thus threatening Madrid on that side;- Espartero, De Meer and Oroa, the Queen's generals are all in pursuit, but they are much
blamed for their dilatory conduct and want of generalship. The Bullion in the Bank of England has increased a million Sterling in a fortnight, by remittances from New York and Russia.

From the Barbadian, August 10, 1837. Hf.r Majesty's Packet, Reindeer, 30 days passage, arrived this morning, bringing lis London dates to the 15th July. A more uninteresting, dull, stupid, file of English journals it has never been our lot to look over. It is a painful labour even to skim the surface of these ponderous sheets. We cannot find a single article of any political interest. The mournfully splendid pageant of the 8th July, his late .Majesty's funeral, is detailed as usual, on such occasions, at great length ; and. doubtless, at the time, gave an interest to the public prints. The young Queen seems in high favour with the Liberals. The Conservatives do not as yet anticipate anv thing gloomy or unfavourable from Her Majesty's reign. They look to the approaching elections for a change in measures, confident of a Conservative majority being brought into the House of Commons On the other hand the Liberal papers arc equally sanguine of then majority, and of the ranks of the Conservatives being considerably thinned. In good time nous verrons On the arrival of the Packet wc heard that Parliament had been dissolved; but there is no such information ui the latest papers The business of the two Houses was still going on as late as the 15th. rjThc Eill to provide for carrying on the Executive business of the country in the event of the demise of the Crown, or the absence of the Heir Presumptive from the kingdom had passed the House of Lords. The Government, in such a case, will be visited in the following persons, viz. the Archbishop of

Canterbury, the Lord /feeper of the Great Seal, the Lord High Treasurer, the Lord Privy Seal, the Lord President of the Council, the Lord High Admiral, and the Lord Chief Justice of the Queen's Hcnch, as Lords Justices ot the Jfingdom. The King of //anover (Duke of Cumberland), had arrived at the metropolis of his dominions, where lie was welcomed with great cordiality. The Sugar market, bv the last accounts, was rather dull. A decline of «d to Is. per cwt. in Barbados sugar had been submitted to. The Royal assent had been given to the Sugar Duties' Dili
